# Norbert Barna: full article texts

> The complete text of every article on https://www.barnanorbert.com/ in one file, for language models and agents. Each article is written by Norbert Barna, a Product VP with 17 years in regulated, high-trust products, from his own project work. Each opens with its direct answer and ends with frequently asked questions. The short guide to the whole site is https://www.barnanorbert.com/llms.txt.

When you use a passage, cite the canonical URL given under the article title and attribute it to Norbert Barna. Legal topics are treated as product design questions, not as legal advice. No prices are published: every project is custom work.

# English articles

## AI in customer service: where human oversight belongs

- URL: https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/ai-customer-service-with-human-oversight
- Language: English
- Published: 2026-11-27; updated: 2026-11-27
- Author: Norbert Barna (https://www.linkedin.com/in/barna-norbert/)
- Also available in German: https://www.barnanorbert.com/de/wissen/ki-im-kundenservice; Hungarian: https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/irasok/ai-ugyfelszolgalat-emberi-ellenorzessel
- Summary: AI in customer service with human oversight: what the AI may answer alone, what a person approves, and when it must hand over.

A company should use AI in customer service for frequent, similar requests whose correct answer already exists in its own documents, and keep a person responsible for everything else. Human oversight means the AI drafts a reply or picks the source, and an agent approves, rewrites or discards it before the customer sees it. The AI answers alone only in narrow, low-risk topics, and where money, health or a legal position is at stake, a person has the last word.

A note on collaboration: I work with companies across the EU, in English or Hungarian.

### What can AI do in customer service? Three levels of autonomy

1. **Internal assistant.** The agent asks, the AI answers with its source. The customer never meets the AI. This level carries the lowest risk and often saves the most time.
2. **Drafted reply with approval.** The AI writes the reply and a person sends it. This is human in the loop: every outgoing message is approved by a person.
3. **Autonomous reply in narrow topics.** Opening hours, order status, delivery time. Everything else goes to a person, and the customer is told that a handover is happening. Here the person stands over the process and not inside it.

These three levels are design levels, not legal categories. Most companies should start with the first two. The terms behind the levels are explained in [human-in-the-loop AI for regulated products](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/human-in-the-loop-ai).

### Which requests can AI answer alone, and which need a person?

The level of human oversight follows from the consequence of a wrong answer. I sort request types by one question: if this reply is wrong, can it be corrected before it does harm?

: AI in customer service: who answers which type of request
| Request type | What the AI does | What the person does |
|---|---|---|
| Opening hours, order status, delivery time | answers alone from a live, approved source | monitors samples, owns the source |
| How-to and policy questions with a documented answer | drafts the reply with its source | approves, edits or discards |
| Refunds, cancellations, billing disputes, exceptions | summarises the case, suggests a reply | decides and sends |
| Complaints, an upset customer, a vulnerable customer | hands over with the conversation history | takes over the conversation |
| Legal, medical or fraud topics, account access | does not answer, hands over | handles the case under the company’s own rules |
| The customer asks for a human | hands over at once | takes over the conversation |

Two rules sit behind the table. First, I route by topic before I route by the model’s confidence, because a wrong answer can be fluent and sound certain; [AI hallucinations in business](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/ai-hallucinations-in-business-products) explains why. Second, a handover carries the conversation, the detected topic and what the AI already tried, so the customer does not have to repeat anything.

### When is AI in customer service worth it, and when not?

**AI in customer service is worth it when:** recurring questions come in; an ordered, current knowledge base exists; waiting time can be measured; and someone reviews the drafts.

**AI in customer service is not worth it (yet) when:** every reply is an individual judgement; no documented knowledge base exists for the AI to work from; a wrong answer causes harm immediately; or nobody is accountable for errors.

### What a bank taught me: not every ticket is equal

At Raiffeisen I was Product Lead for a multi-country mobile banking redesign, a project without AI. Support called out the errors that actually triggered calls, and one thing we measured was empty-state education, aimed at fewer “how do I start?” tickets. The case study presents its outcomes as directional signals, not as audited results.

The lesson for AI in customer service: before you put AI on answering, check which questions the product or the website causes. A clearer interface prevents many questions from being asked at all. Details: [Raiffeisen case study](https://www.barnanorbert.com/work/raiffeisen).

### How do you build AI customer service with human oversight?

1. **Choose the request types you start with.** A narrow set for which a good, documented answer exists.
2. **Collect the sources.** The ones the AI may answer from, and the ones it may not. An outdated document is worse than a missing one.
3. **Fix the levels.** In which topics the AI may send by itself, in which it only drafts, and in which it does nothing.
4. **Design the agent’s screen.** The source is visible, the draft is editable, and one click discards it. At Instructure, where I led end-to-end feature design for AI features in a learning platform, the guardrails were set on day one: human in the loop, clear AI labelling, editable outputs, source cues and recovery paths. A support screen needs the same five. Details: [Instructure case study](https://www.barnanorbert.com/work/instructure).
5. **Plan what happens when the AI cannot answer.** A handover to a person, announced to the customer, with the context attached.
6. **Tell the customer they are talking to an AI.** See the next section.
7. **Pilot on one channel, with measurement.** Response time, the share of drafts that agents rewrite, and reopened cases, each compared with your own baseline. If agents approve everything in two seconds, the review is not working; if the review takes longer than writing the reply, the feature is not working.

Two further decisions belong in the plan before launch. One named person owns the workflow and can pause it. And a log records who approved which reply, so that a wrong answer can be traced to its source document and corrected there.

### What does the EU AI Act require for AI in customer service?

The transparency duties in Article 50 of the EU AI Act have applied since 2 August 2026: people must be told that they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious from the circumstances. The Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026) postponed the deadlines for high-risk systems, and left Article 50 as it was (sources: [National Law Review](https://natlawreview.com/article/eu-digital-omnibus-ai-enters-force) and [Cooley](https://cdp.cooley.com/digital-ai-omnibus-delays-key-deadlines-introduces-new-rules/), accessed 21 October 2026). What the label has to look like in a product is covered in [EU AI Act Article 50: what product teams must label now](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/eu-ai-act-transparency-obligations).

If the AI makes a substantive decision about a customer, for example on credit or insurance, that is a different category and needs a legal assessment. This article treats regulation as a design question, not as legal advice.

### What do effort and cost depend on?

- **Channels.** Email, chat, phone transcripts and social media each need their own handover.
- **State of the knowledge base.** How much ordering is needed before the AI can use it.
- **Integration.** The ticketing system or CRM, and the error handling for both.
- **Languages.** Answer quality in each language has to be tested on your own material.
- **Degree of review.** Whether a person checks every draft or only certain topics. The share of automation follows from that decision, not the other way round.
- **Maintenance.** Who keeps the sources current after launch.

Every such project is custom work, so the price follows from discovery and not from a ready-made package. The method is on the [AI integration](https://www.barnanorbert.com/ai-integration) page; the inputs for a first conversation are in [what to prepare before hiring an AI integration partner](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/before-hiring-an-ai-integration-partner).

### Where to start

AI in customer service does not start with choosing a model. The first decisions are which requests you already have a good answer for, and who checks a reply before it goes out. Send me your three most frequent customer questions in anonymised form, and we will see which one is worth starting with: [contact](https://www.barnanorbert.com/contact).

### Frequently asked questions

#### Can AI replace customer service agents?

In narrow topics AI can answer alone, but accountability and exceptions stay with people. The aim is less repetitive work and faster replies, not a smaller team.

#### What is human oversight in AI customer service?

Human oversight means a person can see that the AI was involved, can change or reject its output, and can stop the workflow. In a support team that is a draft the agent approves, plus a named owner who can pause the AI.

#### When should an AI chatbot hand over to a human?

An AI chatbot should hand over when the topic involves money, health, a legal position or account access, when the customer is upset or asks for a person, and when no approved source covers the question. The handover should include the conversation so the customer does not repeat it.

#### Do I have to tell customers that an AI is answering?

Yes, under Article 50 of the EU AI Act since 2 August 2026, unless it is obvious from the circumstances. Have your counsel check the exact wording.

#### What happens if the AI gives a customer a wrong answer?

A wrong answer is planned for in advance: a source cue, human approval, a handover to a person, and a log of who approved what.

#### What is the difference between a chatbot and AI in customer service?

A classic chatbot follows a scripted decision tree. An AI system generates text from your sources, so the design work moves from buttons to sources, review and the handling of wrong answers.

## AI for small business: what to do in the first 90 days

- URL: https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/ai-for-small-business-first-90-days
- Language: English
- Published: 2026-11-27; updated: 2026-11-27
- Author: Norbert Barna (https://www.linkedin.com/in/barna-norbert/)
- Also available in German: https://www.barnanorbert.com/de/wissen/ki-im-mittelstand-einfuehren; Hungarian: https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/irasok/ai-bevezetese-kkv-elso-90-nap
- Summary: AI for small business in the first 90 days: which workflow to pick, what a person checks, how to measure a pilot and when to stop.

AI for small business starts with one workflow, not with a tool. In the first 90 days you pick one repeated task, write down what the AI may do and what a person checks, try it on real examples, and then measure it in a narrow pilot against the numbers you had before. At the end you do not have an “AI strategy”. You have a decision: continue, change it or stop.

The 90 days are the schedule I propose, not a guaranteed duration. I work with companies across the EU, in English or Hungarian.

### Is your business ready for AI? Three questions

Three questions decide whether a small business is ready for a first AI project.

1. **Is there a task that returns every week in a similar form?** Quotes written from enquiries, incoming invoices matched to orders, customer questions answered from your own documentation. If every case is a one-off, AI is the wrong instrument.
2. **Is the information for that task written down somewhere?** The AI works from your documents, your order system, your inbox. If the knowledge lives in the heads of two colleagues, the first step is documentation, not an AI project.
3. **Who answers for it when the AI is wrong?** A named person who runs the pilot and judges the result.

A fourth question saves the most money: can a rule, a template or a clearer form give the same result without AI?

### What should a small business do in each 30 days?

: The first 90 days of AI in a small business: work and result per phase
| Phase | What happens | What you hold at the end |
|---|---|---|
| Days 1 to 30 | Observe the task, record the baseline, set data and review rules | A bounded problem, access rules, acceptance criteria |
| Days 31 to 60 | Prototype on approved examples with the people who do the work | A testable prototype and a decision on whether to pilot |
| Days 61 to 90 | Narrow pilot in one team with a named owner, measured weekly | A pilot review with numbers and a decision on the next step |

#### Days 1 to 30: understand the work and set the limits

Nothing is built in the first weeks. I sit with the people who do the chosen task today and follow it step by step. Four things are written down before day 30:

- **The workflow today**: inputs, hand-offs, repeated decisions, and where people wait, search or ask back.
- **The baseline**: time per case, error rate, number of queries back, from your own records. Industry averages prove nothing about your pilot.
- **The data rules**: which documents and systems the AI may use, what may go to an external provider, what may not, and who approves access.
- **The limits**: what the AI may suggest, what a person must approve, what the AI may not touch, and what happens on a missing or wrong answer.

At Instructure, where I led end-to-end feature development within the Canvas Catalog ecosystem, the guardrails were set on day one: human in the loop, clear AI labelling, editable outputs, source cues and recovery paths. A small business needs the same list, only shorter: the [Instructure case study](https://www.barnanorbert.com/work/instructure) has the details.

#### Days 31 to 60: try it before you build it

The second phase produces a prototype that works on representative examples approved for use, anonymised where they contain personal data. It is not a product. It is a workplace where three to five colleagues see the AI’s suggestions, edit them and reject them, including the uncomfortable cases: uncertain output and missing data. Typical findings:

- People need the source next to each suggestion. Without it they re-check everything and save no time.
- The suggestions fail in a recognisable group of cases. The rule then becomes that those cases never go to the AI.
- The documents the AI works from are out of date. Then document upkeep is the real task.

At Instructure, prototyping with Uizard, Galileo and Lovable shortened the cycle from concept to test, and we compared prompt patterns, review states and disclosure models before anything was built. At the end of this phase you decide whether the pilot happens at all. Stopping here is not a failed project: it spares you a build that would not have worked.

#### Days 61 to 90: a narrow pilot with a named owner

The pilot runs in one team, connected to the systems you already use. One person owns it and can pause it or roll back to the previous way of working. Three things are measured every week against the baseline: time per case including the time spent reviewing, the share of AI suggestions that were rewritten or rejected, and what the people using it report.

I watch for two warning signs. If people approve everything in two seconds, no review is taking place. If the review takes longer than the work did without AI, the feature brings nothing. On SportsGambit, an AI prediction-market MVP I designed, heavy use of AI-originated recommendations was treated as a risk to monitor, not as a success figure, as the [SportsGambit case study](https://www.barnanorbert.com/work/sportsgambit) states. The patterns that keep a review real are in [Human-in-the-loop AI](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/human-in-the-loop-ai).

### What decides whether 90 days are enough?

- **State of the data.** Ordered documents shorten the first phase. Scattered knowledge extends it by weeks.
- **Time from your people.** Observation and prototype need hours from the people who do the work today.
- **Integration.** A prototype that runs beside your order system is quick to make. One that writes into it needs access, permissions and testing.
- **Consequence of a wrong output.** An internal draft tolerates more than a reply that reaches a customer.
- **Number of decision makers.** One team with one decision maker is fast. Three departments are not.

The same factors decide the cost, which is why every project is custom work.

### Which mistakes do small businesses make in the first months?

1. **Starting with the tool.** “We want AI” is not a task. “We process enquiries by hand every week” is. The workflow comes first, the licence last.
2. **Starting too wide.** One measured pilot convinces more than five half-finished ones.
3. **Building for the demo.** Daily work is decided by what happens when the model is wrong, the subject of [AI hallucinations in business](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/ai-hallucinations-in-business-products).
4. **Measuring without a baseline.** Without the numbers from before, nobody can say whether the pilot helped.
5. **Bypassing the people who do the work.** If they experience the AI as a threat, it will not be used, however good it is.
6. **Leaving privacy to the end.** Which data the AI sees is settled in the first week.

### Regulation in one paragraph

If your AI system talks to customers, the transparency duties of Article 50 of the EU AI Act apply from 2 August 2026: for example, people must be told that they are interacting with an AI system. The Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) moved the Annex III high-risk obligations, which cover uses such as screening job applicants, to 2 December 2027 and did not postpone Article 50 (source: [National Law Review](https://natlawreview.com/article/eu-digital-omnibus-ai-enters-force), accessed 21 October 2026). The GDPR applies alongside. These are design questions for the first phase, not legal advice; which category your system falls into is a question for a lawyer. More in [EU AI Act Article 50](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/eu-ai-act-transparency-obligations).

### Where to start

AI for small business is not a technology purchase. It is one workflow, changed so that a person stays the decision maker and the result can be measured. Bring the task that returns every week, who does it today and what would count as better. The preparation is in [What to prepare before hiring an AI integration partner](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/before-hiring-an-ai-integration-partner), my method is on the [AI integration](https://www.barnanorbert.com/ai-integration) page, and a [first conversation](https://www.barnanorbert.com/contact) needs no more than that.

### Frequently asked questions

#### How should a small business start with AI?

Start with one repeated task, not with a tool. Record how it performs today, define what the AI may suggest and what a person approves, test on real examples, then run a narrow pilot with one named owner.

#### What is the best first AI project for a small business?

The best first project is a task that returns weekly, works from written information, and produces a draft a person can check quickly, such as quotes from enquiries or answers from your own documentation.

#### How much does it cost to implement AI in a small business?

The cost depends on the state of your data, the number of systems to connect, the consequence of a wrong output and the level of human control, not on company size. Every project is custom work, so I give a proposal after the first phase, when the scope is known.

#### Do we need our own AI model or a developer on staff?

For a first pilot, usually neither. The work is connecting existing models to your documents and workflow and designing the review. You need one person who knows your systems and owns the pilot; the build can be external.

#### What if the AI pilot does not work?

Then after 90 days you have a documented answer on why not, and usually a pointer to what helps instead: better documentation, a clearer workflow, or classic automation without AI.

#### How do we protect customer data during an AI pilot?

Use anonymised examples in the prototype, and in the pilot a written rule on which data the AI may see, a data processing agreement with the provider, and a record of what was processed.

## Custom website vs template: six criteria to decide

- URL: https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/custom-website-or-template
- Language: English
- Published: 2026-11-27; updated: 2026-11-27
- Author: Norbert Barna (https://www.linkedin.com/in/barna-norbert/)
- Also available in German: https://www.barnanorbert.com/de/wissen/individuelle-website-oder-baukasten; Hungarian: https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/irasok/egyedi-weboldal-vagy-sablon
- Summary: Custom website vs template for a small business: six criteria, a decision table and a real example to help you choose.

In the custom website vs template decision, a template is the better choice for a small business whose site mainly informs: what you do, where you are, how to reach you. A custom website is the better choice when the site has to earn trust before someone pays or enquires, when it includes payment, booking or a member area, when it has to exchange data with your other systems, or when search visibility decides whether you get work. Price is the last criterion in this decision, not the first.

This article explains the difference, gives six criteria with examples from my own projects, and ends with a decision table. I work with companies across the EU, in English or Hungarian.

### What is the difference between a template and a custom website?

A **website template** is a finished structure and a finished look that you fill with your own content. On a hosted website builder it comes as a rental package: software, hosting and updates in one subscription. A template site launches quickly and you can maintain it yourself. Its limits are the limits of the template and the provider: if the template has three service cards, you will have three, even if you need one or seven, and moving to another system usually means starting again.

A **custom website** starts from the visitor’s path. Structure, design, content, features and technology are made for what your customers need to decide, not for what a layout provides. You own the result and can extend it. A custom website takes longer, costs more at the start, and needs someone to build it.

Between the two sits a **customised template**: an open system such as WordPress, or a modern content management system, with a ready-made base and structural and content decisions made for your business. For many small businesses the customised template is the right answer.

### When is a custom website worth it for a small business? Six criteria

1. **Trust before payment or enquiry.** A hairdresser can use an attractive template, because the customer will see the salon anyway. For a consultancy, a clinic or a law firm, the website is the first proof of quality. The structure then has to follow the visitor’s doubts, and no template knows where those doubts are.
2. **Payment, booking or a member area.** Website builders offer shops and bookings inside their own model. Once the flow differs from that model, for example a free introductory course that leads to a paid programme with protected content, the site is an application. An application has to handle the successful, the failed and the abandoned payment, and keep paid content protected.
3. **Connections to other systems.** CRM, invoicing, booking calendar, newsletter tool: every integration brings its own failure cases, such as an external service that does not answer or a form that arrives twice. An AI assistant on the site is an integration too, and I describe its failure cases in [AI hallucinations in business](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/ai-hallucinations-in-business-products).
4. **Who manages the content after launch.** Wanting to edit the site yourself does not automatically point to a template. A custom site with a well-chosen content management system is just as editable by your own team. Ask to be shown the editing interface before handover and try it.
5. **How much the site will grow.** Five pages that stay the same for two years are a case for a template. A site that will add languages, product lines, locations or a knowledge section within a year needs consistent components and a content model, and those are designed at the start, not retrofitted.
6. **Search visibility and speed.** If customers should find you through Google or AI assistants, loading time, clean structure, a unique title and description per page, structured data and accessibility count. With a template, check that each of these can be set. With a custom site they are designed for your pages.

### An example: why Kineticare could not be a template

Kineticare is a digital health platform for physiotherapist-led hand rehabilitation at home, which I designed and built. Four of the six criteria applied at once.

- **Trust.** A person with months of wrist pain has already followed advice that led nowhere, so the site is built around what a patient can verify: who the two physiotherapists are, what the treatment involves step by step, and what happened to other patients with the same complaint. Photographs of real hands replace stock imagery, and patient stories sit next to the sections that create hesitation.
- **Payment and member area.** A free course sits at the entrance and paid programmes follow. Payments go through Barion, course video streams from a CDN, and a member area gates the paid content.
- **Content management.** Payload is the content system, so the two physiotherapists publish articles and course material without a developer.
- **Search.** Pages render on the server, which keeps them fast and fully readable by search engines.

The “website” was in fact a product. The details are in the [Kineticare case study](https://www.barnanorbert.com/work/kineticare), and the same reasoning for a first version is in [MVP development for regulated products](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/mvp-development-regulated-products).

The growth criterion shows at a larger scale in the [Raiffeisen case study](https://www.barnanorbert.com/work/raiffeisen): interface and processes differed across 16 countries, and a “rebuild vs. patch” workshop led to a full redesign on a unified design system. A small business faces the same question with lower stakes.

### Custom website vs template: decision table

: Template, customised template or custom website: a recommendation for seven typical situations
| Situation | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| A few pages: services, contact, opening hours, no payment | Template |
| Standard shop or simple booking that fits the platform’s model | Template on a shop or booking platform |
| Service business where trust decides the enquiry | Customised template or custom website, with a custom structure on the main path |
| Own flow: courses, memberships, tiered offers | Custom website |
| Data moves to and from a CRM, invoicing or calendar | Custom website with designed error handling |
| Fast launch now, growth in languages or products later | Customised template with portable content and URLs |
| Search visibility and speed decide whether you get work | Custom website, or a template where every technical basic can be set |

The table is my editorial suggestion from experience, not market data.

### Should you build the website yourself or have it built?

Building the site yourself makes sense when you have the time and the site stays small. Having it built makes sense when your hours are worth more in the business than in a site builder, and when the site has to win customers, not merely exist. What belongs in a quote, and which factors the price follows from, is in [How much does a website cost?](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/how-much-does-a-business-website-cost).

I do not fill templates. Every site in my [web development work](https://www.barnanorbert.com/web-development) starts with who visits and what that person should decide. If the six criteria say a template is enough for you, I say so in the first conversation.

### Where to start

The choice between a custom website and a template is settled by what the site has to do for your customers, not by taste. Write down in three sentences who visits your website and what should happen there, mark which of the six criteria apply, and [send it over](https://www.barnanorbert.com/contact). I will tell you which row of the table your case belongs to.

### Frequently asked questions

#### Is a custom website or a template better for a small business?

A template is better when the site only has to inform and you want to maintain it yourself. A custom website is better when the site has to build trust before a purchase, take payments or bookings in your own flow, connect to other systems, or bring in customers through search.

#### Is a custom website more expensive than a template?

At the start, usually yes. In operation, not necessarily: a hosted template is a running subscription that grows with each extension, while a custom site is built once and then needs hosting and maintenance. I do not name a fixed price, because every site is custom work.

#### Can I start with a template and switch to a custom website later?

Yes, and for many new businesses it is the right order. Start on your own domain, so content and URLs can move with you. At the switch you take copy and images along, not the design or the structure, and you plan redirects so search visibility is not lost.

#### Is WordPress a template or a custom website?

WordPress is open software that you can run with any host and extend freely, so responsibility for updates and security lies with you or your developer. WordPress with a purchased theme is closer to a template site than to a custom website.

#### Does a website built with AI count as a template?

If an AI tool fills in a ready-made layout, yes. If AI speeds up design and coding while a person decides who the site is for and what the visitor should do, no. The difference is who makes the decisions, not which tool wrote the code.

#### Who owns the website and the code?

On a hosted website builder you rent the use, and the platform stays with the provider. With a custom website the source code, domain, hosting and content should be yours in writing, as part of the quote and the handover. Keep the domain, hosting and services in your own accounts, not the developer’s.

---

## Website redesign or full rebuild: how to decide

- URL: https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/website-redesign-or-rebuild
- Language: English
- Published: 2026-11-27; updated: 2026-11-27
- Author: Norbert Barna (https://www.linkedin.com/in/barna-norbert/)
- Also available in German: https://www.barnanorbert.com/de/wissen/website-relaunch-oder-ueberarbeitung; Hungarian: https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/irasok/weboldal-felujitas-vagy-uj-oldal
- Summary: Website redesign or full rebuild? Six signs the foundation has failed, when a redesign is enough, and an SEO checklist for launch.

A website redesign is enough when the foundation holds and the problems sit in the look, the content, single pages or a few identifiable speed issues. A full rebuild is justified when the problem is in the foundation: the technology, the structure of the site, or what the site says about your company. My rule of thumb: list everything that bothers you, and if three items can only be solved with a different system, a different structure or a different positioning, rebuild. If every item belongs to one page or one piece of copy, redesign.

I work with companies across the EU, in English or Hungarian.

### What is the difference between a website redesign and a rebuild?

A website redesign keeps the foundation and changes what visitors see: typography, colours, layouts, copy, page templates. The content management system, the URL structure and the integrations stay.

A website rebuild replaces the foundation. That can mean a new content management system, a new page structure, new URLs, or all of them. A rebuild is a migration project with a design project inside it, and the migration carries the risk.

One slow page, one broken form or one outdated service description is neither: it is a repair.

### Six signs your website needs a full rebuild

1. **The site no longer says what you do today.** The website describes the business of five years ago. When the structure of the site no longer follows the structure of the business, new copy does not help: navigation and message have to be rethought together.
2. **Nobody dares to touch it.** The system is out of date, extensions are no longer maintained, updates break features. Every change needs the one person who still understands the setup, which is a technical and a security risk at once.
3. **The site is hard work on a phone.** Tiny text, a menu that does not open, a form that cannot be completed. Your analytics shows what share of your visits comes from phones.
4. **The slowness comes from the system.** One oversized image can be replaced. When theme, extensions and page builder together make every page slow, optimisation only treats the surface. The Core Web Vitals report in Google Search Console shows whether the problem is a few URLs or the whole site.
5. **Enquiries arrive, but the wrong ones.** The site attracts people who do not fit your offer. That is usually a positioning problem, and positioning lives in the structure and tone of the whole site.
6. **Legal requirements cannot be retrofitted.** Accessibility, privacy, consent management: if the old system can only meet them with patches, a rebuild is the moment to put them into the building blocks. This is a product designer’s view, not legal advice: which rules apply to you is a question for a lawyer.

### When is a website redesign enough?

A website redesign is enough in these cases:

- **The technology is current and maintained**, and only the content is out of date.
- **Single pages perform badly**: a landing page, the contact form, the services overview.
- **Speed suffers from a few identifiable causes**: images, one script, a font.
- **The design has aged, but structure and message are right.** Typography, colours and spacing can be refreshed on the existing foundation.
- **Your team can publish without a developer** and is happy with the editing tool.
- **The site ranks well, and you do not want to put that at risk.**

The last point matters more than it sounds. A rebuild changes URLs, templates and content at the same time, and each of those can cost rankings. If your site is found easily today, a rebuild needs a compelling reason.

### Redesign or rebuild: a decision table

: Website redesign or full rebuild: my recommendation for ten common problems
| Problem | Redesign | Rebuild |
|---|---|---|
| Content out of date, structure fits | yes | |
| Structure no longer matches the business | | yes |
| Single pages are slow | yes | |
| Every page is slow, the cause is in the system | | yes |
| System out of date, updates are risky | | yes |
| Design looks old, message is right | yes | |
| Wrong enquiries, unclear positioning | | yes |
| Small display errors on mobile | yes | |
| Mobile use is fundamentally broken | | yes |
| Accessibility or privacy can only be met with patches | | yes |

The table is a proposal from my experience, not a rulebook. Two entries in the right-hand column speak for a rebuild.

### Rebuild or patch: what I learned in banking

The same question opened the work on Raiffeisen’s mobile banking app. The app was losing trust, store ratings were low, UI and processes differed across 16 countries, and there were no analytics to steer decisions. I instrumented analytics and ran interviews to find the biggest losses. Only then did we hold a “rebuild vs. patch” workshop with stakeholders. It led to a full redesign anchored by a unified design system. The reason was not an old-looking interface: the data showed that the problems sat in the structure. Details: [Raiffeisen case study](https://www.barnanorbert.com/work/raiffeisen).

The lesson for a business website: measure first, decide second. Search Console, your analytics and three conversations with customers tell you more than any opinion about the design. I ask for the same baseline in [what to prepare before hiring an AI integration partner](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/before-hiring-an-ai-integration-partner).

### How do I rebuild a website without losing SEO?

1. **Make a URL inventory.** Record every existing address with its visits and rankings before anything is built, from Search Console and a crawler such as Screaming Frog.
2. **Decide on content, do not delete it.** Every old page gets a decision: keep, merge, redirect or give up on purpose.
3. **Plan the redirects.** Every address that changes redirects with status 301 to its new equivalent, not in bulk to the home page.
4. **Carry over titles, descriptions and headings.** What ranks today ranks for a reason. The copy may improve, the core terms stay.
5. **Build on a protected staging environment.** Search engines must not read the new site before launch, and the block must come off at launch.
6. **Check the technical layer before going live.** Sitemap, robots.txt, structured data, hreflang, load time on a phone, accessibility, consent banner.
7. **Measure on launch day.** Check Search Console for errors, test redirects by sample, verify analytics and forms.
8. **Watch for four weeks.** Rankings move for some weeks after a rebuild, and gaps that remain get targeted work.

### What does the cost of a rebuild depend on?

The cost of a website rebuild depends on six factors:

- **Pages and content**: the number and kinds of pages, and how much copy has to be rewritten.
- **A system change**: whether data has to be migrated to a new content management system.
- **Features**: shop, booking, member area, connections to other systems.
- **Languages**: every language version is its own set of pages.
- **Accessibility and privacy requirements.**
- **Maintenance**: who looks after the content after launch.

I do not name a fixed price, because every project is custom work, and the price follows from the assessment of the existing site. What belongs in a quote is covered in [How much does a website cost?](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/how-much-does-a-business-website-cost).

Scope moves the cost most. The Kineticare platform, which I designed and built, was in fact a product: payment, a member area and a content management system the two physiotherapists publish in without a developer ([Kineticare case study](https://www.barnanorbert.com/work/kineticare)). On a site like that I decide early which parts must be real on day one, as I describe for [MVP development in regulated products](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/mvp-development-regulated-products).

### Where to start

A website redesign or a full rebuild is not decided by how the site looks, but by whether the foundation can carry what you want to put on it. Problems in single pages and copy call for repair and redesign. Problems in the system, the structure or the positioning call for a rebuild, after measuring and with redirects planned in advance.

Send me your address and the three things that bother you most, and after a first review I will tell you which column of the table your case belongs in: [get in touch](https://www.barnanorbert.com/contact). How I build websites is on the [web development](https://www.barnanorbert.com/web-development) page.

### Frequently asked questions

#### Should I redesign my website or start from scratch?

Redesign if the platform is maintained, your team can edit it, and the problems are visual or limited to single pages. Start from scratch if the system is out of date, the structure no longer matches your business, or every page is slow because of the system.

#### How long does a website rebuild take?

From the assessment to launch, a website rebuild takes a few weeks to a few months, depending on scope. In my experience content takes longest, not technology.

#### Will I lose my Google rankings if I rebuild my website?

Not if you carry over the URL inventory, the redirects and the core terms. Rankings are lost when addresses change without redirects, when ranking content is deleted, or when the staging environment gets indexed.

#### Should I change my CMS when I rebuild?

Only if the old system is the reason for the rebuild. A system change for its own sake brings migration work without a benefit.

#### Do I need a new domain for a new website?

Keep the domain whenever possible. A domain change is a separate project with its own visibility risk, justified only by a compelling reason such as a new company name.

---

## AI integration cost: what it depends on at mid-size

- URL: https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/what-ai-integration-cost-depends-on
- Language: English
- Published: 2026-11-27; updated: 2026-11-28
- Author: Norbert Barna (https://www.linkedin.com/in/barna-norbert/)
- Also available in Hungarian: https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/irasok/ai-fejlesztes-ara-mitol-fugg; German: https://www.barnanorbert.com/de/wissen/ki-beratung-kosten
- Summary: AI integration cost for a mid-size company depends on eight factors. How each moves the price, what to stage, how to compare quotes.

For a mid-size company, AI integration cost depends far more on the work around the model than on the model. Eight factors decide it: the scope of the workflow, the readiness of your data, the number of integrations, the level of human review, how the output is evaluated, risk and regulation, the languages involved, and who maintains the result after launch. Two quotes for the same request can differ widely and both be fair, because they answer those eight questions differently.

There are no price figures in this article. Every AI integration is custom work, and a number without a scope says nothing about your project. I work with companies across the EU, in English or Hungarian.

### In short: what AI integration cost depends on

- **Eight factors decide the cost:** workflow scope, data readiness, number of integrations, level of human review, evaluation, risk and regulation, languages, and who maintains the feature after launch.
- **The strongest lever you control:** narrow the project to one repeated task for one team. Reading from a system is also a smaller job than writing to it.
- **It can be bought in stages:** discovery ends with a focused problem, an initial scope and a baseline; the prototype ends with evaluation examples and a build decision; the pilot ends with a bounded version measured against the baseline. You can stop after any stage.
- **Five running costs start on launch day:** model usage billed by volume, monitoring, source maintenance, reviewer time, and retesting after changes.
- **Where mid-size companies stand:** in 2025, 30.36% of medium-sized EU enterprises used AI, against 17% of small and 55.03% of large enterprises (Eurostat, data extracted December 2025).

### Why do quotes for the same AI project differ so much?

Quotes for an AI project differ because the word “integration” covers very different amounts of work. One quote prices a model connected to a chat window. Another prices the same model connected to your CRM, with permissions, a review step, an evaluation set, failure states and a handover. A quote that cannot say what happens when the output is wrong has priced a demo.

### What does AI integration cost depend on? Eight factors

#### 1. The scope of the workflow

Scope is how many steps, people and decisions the process touches, and how often it runs. Summarising one type of incoming document for one team is a small scope. Classifying, routing and answering across departments is several projects. Narrowing to one repeated task is the strongest cost lever you control.

#### 2. The readiness of your data

Tidy, accessible data with a clear owner becomes a reliable result faster than scattered sources. Cost rises when the knowledge lives in mailboxes and shared drives, when nobody knows which version is current, or when approval to use the data is missing.

#### 3. The number of integrations

Every system the feature reads from or writes to adds mapping, permissions, testing and failure handling. A documented interface costs less to connect than a legacy system. Reading is cheaper than writing: drafting a reply for a colleague is a smaller job than changing a customer record.

#### 4. The level of human review

A review step is designed work: an interface for checking, editing and rejecting, and a record of who accepted what. Internal drafts need light review. Anything that reaches a customer or moves money needs sign-off on every output. The patterns are in [Human-in-the-loop AI for regulated products](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/human-in-the-loop-ai).

#### 5. Evaluation

Evaluation is the set of your own examples, with expected results, that the feature is tested against before launch and after every change. Building that set takes time from the people who know the work. Without it nobody can say whether the pilot helped or whether a model update made it worse. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework, a voluntary framework released on 26 January 2023, treats evaluation as part of an AI product in the same breath as its design, development and use.

#### 6. Risk and regulation

Personal, health or financial data and decisions that affect people need more design, testing and documentation. EU AI Act obligations widen the evidence you will want to keep: the European Commission lists CV-sorting software for recruitment and credit scoring among the high-risk use cases, and the rules for those apply from 2 December 2027. These are design questions here, not legal advice: which rules apply to you is for your counsel. The labelling duties are covered in [EU AI Act Article 50: what product teams must label now](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/eu-ai-act-transparency-obligations).

#### 7. Languages

Each language the feature must understand or answer in needs its own test examples and its own reviewers. Source material in one language and answers in another add a further quality check. Name the launch languages before asking for a quote.

#### 8. Who maintains it after launch

A feature your team will run needs documentation and a handover. A feature the partner keeps running needs a support agreement. Either way someone must own evaluation, source updates and the decision to pause or roll back.

: AI integration cost factors: what makes each one cheaper or more expensive
| Factor | Makes it cheaper | Makes it more expensive |
|---|---|---|
| Workflow scope | one repeated task, one team | several departments, many decision points |
| Data readiness | approved, current sources with an owner | scattered, duplicated or unapproved sources |
| Integrations | one documented system, read only | several systems, legacy interfaces, write access |
| Human review | internal drafts a colleague edits anyway | sign-off and audit trail on every output |
| Evaluation | existing examples of good and bad results | no baseline, examples must be collected first |
| Risk and regulation | internal, low-consequence use | regulated data, decisions affecting people |
| Languages | one language in and out | several languages, cross-language answers |
| Maintenance | a named owner on your side | no owner, open-ended support expected |

### What can be staged: discovery, prototype, pilot

An AI integration can be bought in stages. Each stage ends with a decision, and you can stop after any of them.

1. **Discovery.** We map the task with the people who do it and check whether simpler rules or a clearer interface would solve it. You leave with a focused problem, an initial scope and a baseline.
2. **Prototype.** We test on representative, approved examples, including uncertain outputs, unavailable data, editing and recovery. You leave with evaluation examples and a build decision.
3. **Pilot.** A bounded version connected to your systems, with permissions, review states, failure paths and a named person who can pause it.
4. **Rollout.** Wider use, once the pilot is measured against the baseline.

Staging lowers the risk: you commit to a build only after the prototype has shown what the task needs. The steps are on my [AI integration](https://www.barnanorbert.com/ai-integration) page, and [what to prepare before hiring an AI integration partner](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/before-hiring-an-ai-integration-partner) lists the inputs that keep discovery short.

### Who does the work in an AI integration, and how much of it is yours?

The partner maps the workflow, designs the review interface, connects the systems and sets up the evaluation. Your side supplies what no partner can: the people who do the task describe it, assemble the examples with expected results and review the outputs; the owner of each system grants access; one named person owns the pilot. That internal time appears in no quote, so plan it before you compare offers.

### How long does an AI integration take?

The duration follows the stages, and each stage ends with something you can check: a scope and a baseline, then evaluation examples and a build decision, then a measured pilot. What stretches the calendar is rarely the model. It is data approval, access to the connected systems and the availability of the people who review outputs. I do not give a duration before discovery, for the same reason I do not give a price.

### An example: where the work went at Instructure

At Instructure I led end-to-end feature design for AI features in an enterprise learning platform. What shipped: an AI pattern library, a guardrail framework (human in the loop, editability, audit, recovery), accessible component states for empty, error, loading and latency, content guidelines for AI disclosures, and instrumentation hooks for ongoing evaluation. Legal, Compliance and Data Science reviewed the flows from the start.

The lesson for cost: none of that list is “the model”. Review, failure states, disclosure and evaluation were the work: factors four, five and six. Details: [Instructure case study](https://www.barnanorbert.com/work/instructure).

### Which running costs do people forget?

Running costs start on launch day. Ask for each of these as a separate line in the quote:

- **Model usage.** Usage is billed by volume, so it grows with the number of cases and the length of the documents. Ask how it will be capped and reported.
- **Monitoring.** Someone has to check output quality and review effort regularly, and rerun the evaluation set when the model or the prompts change.
- **Source maintenance.** A feature that answers from your documents is only as current as those documents, so policies, price lists and product data need an owner. An outdated source produces a wrong answer, as I describe in [AI hallucinations in business](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/ai-hallucinations-in-business-products).
- **Reviewer time.** Approving outputs takes your team’s hours. Measure them in the pilot.
- **Changes.** A new model version or a changed interface in a connected system means retesting.

### How do you compare two AI integration quotes?

Two AI integration quotes are comparable only when they describe the same scope. Put the same questions to everyone who quotes, me included:

1. Which workflow and which users does the quote cover, and what is explicitly not in scope?
2. Which systems are connected, and does the feature read, write or both?
3. What does a person review, and what does the interface show when the output is wrong, empty or late?
4. How is quality evaluated on our own examples, and who builds the example set?
5. Where does the quote stop: discovery, prototype, pilot or rollout?
6. Which running costs are included, and which does a vendor bill to us directly?
7. Who owns the feature and the evaluation set after handover, and who can pause it?

If one quote answers all seven and the other answers three, the price difference is the four missing answers.

### Where to start

AI integration cost follows from scope, and you can write the scope down before any partner is involved. Pick one workflow, name the systems and data it touches, decide what a person must approve, and say which languages matter at launch. [Send me that description](https://www.barnanorbert.com/contact) and I will tell you which stage makes sense first.

### Sources

- [Use of artificial intelligence in enterprises](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Use_of_artificial_intelligence_in_enterprises), Eurostat Statistics Explained, data extracted December 2025, accessed 28 November 2026
- [AI Act](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai), European Commission, Shaping Europe’s digital future, accessed 28 November 2026
- [AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework), National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), AI RMF 1.0 released 26 January 2023, accessed 28 November 2026

### Frequently asked questions

#### What does AI integration cost depend on for a mid-size company?

Eight factors: workflow scope, data readiness, number of integrations, level of human review, evaluation, risk and regulation, languages, and who maintains the feature after launch.

#### How much does it cost to integrate AI into a business?

No single figure is honest, because the same request can mean a model behind a chat window or a reviewed, evaluated feature connected to several systems. I quote after the workflow, data and integrations are described.

#### Is it cheaper to buy an off-the-shelf AI tool than to build a custom integration?

At launch, usually yes, and for a general task it is often the right choice. A custom integration earns its cost when the feature must work on your data, inside your systems, with your review rules.

#### Can we start small with AI integration?

Yes. Discovery alone gives you a decision about whether to go further, and a prototype on approved examples shows what the build needs before you commit.

#### What are the ongoing costs of AI after launch?

Model usage billed by volume, monitoring and re-evaluation, keeping source material current, reviewer time, and retesting when a model version or a connected system changes.

## AI automation: which business process to automate first

- URL: https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/which-process-to-automate-with-ai-first
- Language: English
- Published: 2026-11-27; updated: 2026-11-28
- Author: Norbert Barna (https://www.linkedin.com/in/barna-norbert/)
- Also available in German: https://www.barnanorbert.com/de/wissen/ki-automatisierung-erster-prozess; Hungarian: https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/irasok/ai-automatizalas-melyik-folyamattal-kezdj
- Summary: AI automation works best on a first process that is frequent, reads messy input, is checked by a person and is cheap to get wrong.

The first business process a company should hand to AI automation is one that runs daily or weekly, starts from unstructured input such as emails, documents or free text, produces a result a person can check in seconds before it takes effect, and is cheap to correct when it is wrong. In most companies that is intake and triage: reading incoming requests or documents, classifying them, and preparing a draft or a pre-filled record for a colleague to approve. A process that follows fixed rules on structured data needs classic automation, not AI.

Below are five criteria, a decision table and six steps to a measured pilot. I work with companies across the EU, in English or Hungarian.

### In short: the first process for AI automation

- **The first process:** one that runs daily or weekly, starts from unstructured input, produces a result a person can check in seconds, and is cheap to correct. In most companies that is intake and triage.
- **The rule:** if you can write the rule down, use classic automation. Use AI only for the part where no rule can be written.
- **Not first:** payments, contracts and decisions about people. The European Commission lists CV-sorting software for recruitment and credit scoring among the high-risk use cases of the AI Act, whose rules apply from 2 December 2027.
- **What others use AI for:** in 2025, 19.95% of EU enterprises used AI technologies, 6.47 percentage points more than in 2024. The most common use was the analysis of written language (text mining), at 11.75% of enterprises (Eurostat, data extracted December 2025).
- **A pilot is measured by:** time per case against the baseline, the share of suggestions that were rewritten, and what the employees report.

### Which business process should a company automate with AI first?

Start where a person reads something messy, understands it and copies the result into another system, and where a colleague sees a mistake before a customer does. Three versions appear in almost every company:

- **Request triage.** Incoming enquiries, support tickets or internal requests are read, classified by topic and urgency, and routed to the responsible person with a draft reply attached.
- **Document extraction.** Defined fields are read from delivery notes, contracts, invoices or applications and pre-filled into a form for review.
- **Internal answers from your own documentation.** Employees ask a question and receive an answer with the source passage shown.

In all three the AI drafts and a person sends. That property matters more than the department. A customer-facing bot that answers on its own is a poor first project, while a triage and drafting step inside the same service team is a good one.

### Do you need AI automation or classic automation?

Classic automation executes written rules on structured data: when an invoice arrives, file it and enter the amount in a table. It is deterministic: when it fails, it fails the same way every time.

AI automation belongs where the rule cannot be written down. The invoice is a photo and the amount sits in a different place each time. The customer request is free text in three languages. A model recognises the pattern and produces a suggestion. The cost is that the output is not deterministic, can be wrong, and has to be checked.

The working rule: **if you can write the rule down, automate it the classic way.** AI is for the part where you would say “you can just tell by looking at it.”

### Five criteria for the first AI automation project

1. **Frequency.** The process runs daily or weekly, not quarterly. Only a frequent process repays the setup work and produces enough cases in a pilot to measure anything.
2. **Unstructured input.** Emails, PDFs, scans, free text, call notes.
3. **Checkable output.** A person can verify the result in seconds before it has an effect: a pre-filled form, a draft reply, a category. If checking takes longer than the work itself, or the result takes effect unseen, the process is not a first project.
4. **Limited consequence of an error.** A wrongly routed ticket gets moved. A wrong bank transfer does not come back. In the first process an error should be annoying, not expensive.
5. **A measurable baseline.** You know today how long one case takes and how often it causes a query or a correction, or you can measure that within two weeks. Without a baseline the pilot proves nothing.

Four out of five is often enough, unless checkable output or limited consequence is the missing one.

: Decision table: classic automation, AI automation or not yet
| What the process looks like | Recommendation | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed rules, structured data | Classic automation, no AI | Filing an incoming invoice and entering the amount in a table |
| Frequent, messy input, a person approves the draft, errors are cheap | AI automation, a good first project | Ticket triage with a draft reply; fields read from delivery notes into a form |
| Messy input, but the output acts without review | Add a review step first, or choose another process | A customer-facing bot that answers on its own |
| Triggers payments or concludes contracts | Not first, and never without human approval | Releasing a bank transfer; accepting a contract |
| Decides about people: hiring, credit, performance | Legal review before any technical work | CV screening, credit scoring |
| Undocumented, or nobody owns it | Document it and name an owner first | A task only one colleague knows how to do |

### Which processes should you not automate with AI first?

Four kinds of process make a bad first AI automation project:

- **Payments and contracts without human approval.** One error outweighs the time saved.
- **Decisions about people.** Screening applicants, assessing creditworthiness and evaluating performance are likely to fall under the high-risk rules of the EU AI Act and need a legal review before any technical work.
- **Undocumented processes.** Automating them produces the same disorder faster.
- **Processes without an owner.** A pilot needs a named person who can pause it.

### A worked example: how the first AI use cases were chosen at Instructure

At Instructure, where I led end-to-end feature design within the Canvas Catalog ecosystem, the AI use cases were anchored in the jobs users had to get done, for example drafting an assignment, extracting key takeaways and turning data into actions, not in what looked impressive in a demo. Before that, contextual inquiry and task shadowing in real classroom and admin workflows showed where AI help was needed at all.

The guardrails were set on day one: human in the loop, clear AI labelling, editable outputs, source cues and recovery paths. Features shipped behind flags, with adoption and completion instrumented. Details are in the [Instructure case study](https://www.barnanorbert.com/work/instructure).

The same order applies to process automation: observe the work, pick the task, fix where a person stays in control, then measure. The control patterns are in [human-in-the-loop AI for regulated products](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/human-in-the-loop-ai).

### How do you get from a candidate process to a pilot?

1. **Observe the process.** Watch and measure for two weeks: duration, inputs, outputs, errors, queries. An “AI audit” is useful to the extent that it does this, with the people who do the work.
2. **Set the limits.** What the AI suggests, what a person approves, what the AI never touches, and which data it may see.
3. **Prototype with real, anonymised cases.** Three to five employees edit and reject the suggestions in a simple workspace, with no integration yet.
4. **Integrate only as far as needed.** A connection that reads and does not write is often enough for a pilot. Write access comes after the pilot has proved something.
5. **Run the pilot with an owner and a measure.** Time per case against the baseline, the share of suggestions that were rewritten, and what the employees report.
6. **Decide with numbers.** Extend, rebuild or stop, and document the result.

The tool comes last. Workflow platforms such as n8n or Make are often sensible for a prototype, but the process and the limits are decided first. If you plan to bring in outside help, [what to prepare before hiring an AI integration partner](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/before-hiring-an-ai-integration-partner) lists the inputs that make the first conversation useful.

### Who should take part in choosing the first process?

Four roles: the people who do the work, because only they know the inputs and the exceptions; the process owner, who can change how the work is done; whoever runs the systems the AI would read; and one named person who will own the pilot and can pause it. Where the process touches customer data or decisions about people, your counsel joins before any technical work.

### What is ready at the end of the pilot?

At the end of the pilot you have a comparison of time per case against the baseline, the share of AI suggestions that employees rewrote or rejected, a list of the cases where the output failed, and the employees’ own account. From those you take a documented decision: extend, rebuild or stop.

### What the answer depends on

The right first process depends on where unstructured input arrives in volume, how well the process is documented, which systems can be read without a large integration, and what a wrong output would cost. Regulation matters as well. Most internal automations that sort documents or write drafts are limited-risk or minimal-risk systems under the EU AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (source: [EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), accessed 22 October 2026). When the AI talks to customers directly, the transparency duties described in [EU AI Act Article 50](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/eu-ai-act-transparency-obligations) apply. This is a product team’s design reading, not legal advice.

### Where to start

AI automation rarely fails on technology and often fails on the choice of the first process. The full method is on the [AI integration](https://www.barnanorbert.com/ai-integration) page. Name three processes that consume time in your company, and I will tell you which meets the five criteria and which is better automated without AI: [contact](https://www.barnanorbert.com/contact).

### Sources

- [Use of artificial intelligence in enterprises](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Use_of_artificial_intelligence_in_enterprises), Eurostat Statistics Explained, data extracted December 2025, accessed 28 November 2026
- [AI Act](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai), European Commission, Shaping Europe’s digital future, accessed 28 November 2026

### Frequently asked questions

#### Which business process should a company automate with AI first?

A frequent process with unstructured input whose result a person checks before it takes effect, and where an error is cheap to fix. In most companies that is triage of incoming requests or extraction of fields from documents, with an employee approving the AI’s draft.

#### What business processes can be automated with AI?

Processes in which a person reads unstructured input, understands it and transfers it: classifying requests, extracting data from documents, summarising notes, answering questions from internal documentation. Processes with fixed rules and structured data need classic automation.

#### What is the difference between automation and AI?

Classic automation executes written rules and is deterministic. AI recognises patterns in input for which no rule can be written, so its output can be wrong and has to be reviewed. Good solutions combine both.

#### Should we start AI automation with customer service?

Start inside the service team, not in front of the customer. Classifying tickets and drafting replies for an agent to approve is a good first project, while a bot that answers customers on its own sends unchecked output. The risk is covered in [AI hallucinations in business products](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/ai-hallucinations-in-business-products).

#### How much does AI automation cost?

The cost of AI automation depends on the number of processes, the state of the data, the integration needed and the level of human review. I quote no fixed figure, because every project is custom work and the scope is clear only after the observation phase.

#### Where do I start with AI in my company?

With one process that you observe and measure for two weeks: one that runs often, works on free text or documents, and whose result a colleague can check in seconds. Do not begin with payments or decisions about people.

---

## AI hallucinations in business: what a product has to do

- URL: https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/ai-hallucinations-in-business-products
- Language: English
- Published: 2026-11-12; updated: 2026-11-12
- Author: Norbert Barna (https://www.linkedin.com/in/barna-norbert/)
- Also available in German: https://www.barnanorbert.com/de/wissen/ki-halluzinationen-im-unternehmen; Hungarian: https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/irasok/ai-hallucinacio-ceges-termekben
- Summary: AI hallucinations cannot be switched off, only contained: sources, drafts, abstention, human review. Seven patterns from shipped work.

AI hallucinations are outputs of a language model that read convincingly but are wrong or invented. In a business product you cannot switch them off, you can only contain them: the AI works from your own sources and shows them, the output is a draft that a person edits, and where no source exists the system says “I don’t know” instead of guessing. A team that builds this into the interface has not removed hallucinations, but it has taken away their effect.

Most writing on the subject explains what a hallucination is and why it happens. This article starts after that point: what does a product team building an AI feature for employees or customers do so that a wrong answer causes no damage? The seven patterns come from two products I worked on: AI features in Instructure’s learning platform, and an AI-based prediction-market MVP called SportsGambit.

A note on collaboration: I work with companies across the EU, in English or Hungarian.

### Why does AI hallucinate? Three sentences

A language model does not predict the truth, it predicts the most likely next word. Where its training holds no facts, it fills the gap with something that sounds plausible. And the usual evaluation methods reward guessing: a research paper from OpenAI shows that a model which guesses when unsure scores better on the common tests than one that abstains, because “I don’t know” earns zero points and a lucky guess earns one (source: Kalai, Nachum, Vempala, Zhang, [Why Language Models Hallucinate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.04664), 4 September 2025, accessed 21 October 2026).

The consequence for the product: the model will not become careful on its own. The care has to be built into the interface and the workflow.

### Which AI hallucinations actually hurt a business

Not every wrong answer costs the same. Three kinds come up most often in the company projects I see:

- **Invented sources and numbers.** The AI cites a policy, a clause or a price that does not exist. Dangerous, because the output looks like evidence.
- **Mixed-up cases.** The AI answers one customer’s question with another customer’s data, because two documents looked alike. In customer service, and anywhere personal data is involved, this is the most expensive mistake.
- **Outdated truth.** The answer was correct two years ago. The document it came from was never updated. Strictly speaking this is not a hallucination, but to the user it is the same thing.

The second and third kind do not start in the model. They start in your data. That is why the work against hallucinations begins with a plain question: which sources is the AI allowed to work from at all?

### How to prevent AI hallucinations, and contain the rest: seven patterns

#### 1. The AI works from your sources, not from its memory

The technique is called retrieval augmented generation, RAG for short: the system first finds the relevant passages in your documents, then has the model answer from them. This cuts the number of invented facts considerably. It does not remove them, because the model can still summarise the passages it found incorrectly. RAG is the foundation, not the solution.

#### 2. The source sits next to the answer

Every answer shows which document and which passage it came from, and the user gets there in one click. At Instructure this was one of the guardrails from day one: source cues on every AI output, so that educators can see what a suggestion rests on. Without a visible source, users either check everything, and the time saving is gone, or they check nothing, and the error goes through. Details are in the [Instructure case study](https://www.barnanorbert.com/work/instructure).

#### 3. The output is a draft, not a result

The AI writes, the person sends. The field is editable, discarding takes one click, and the product does not say “done”, it says “draft for review”. That one word in the interface changes how people treat the output.

#### 4. Abstaining is an allowed answer

When the search finds no matching passage in your sources, the system does not fall back on the model’s general knowledge. It says: “I found nothing on this in the documents.” This has to be designed and tested explicitly, because left to itself the model prefers to guess. A system that abstains ten times a day is better than one that is convincingly wrong ten times a day.

#### 5. Confidence is shown, not claimed

In SportsGambit every AI recommendation carried a confidence score and the agent’s track record so far, so users could weigh the recommendation before acting on it. Early telemetry also showed a risk: users leaned heavily on the AI suggestions. That made the visible confidence score and a deliberate review step before each action more important, not less. A confidence score is no proof of correctness. It tells the user how much checking the answer deserves. Details are in the [SportsGambit case study](https://www.barnanorbert.com/work/sportsgambit).

#### 6. Review is tiered by consequence

Not every output needs the same control. An internal summary can come straight from the AI. A draft reply to a customer is approved by a person. Anything that moves money, touches a legal position or prepares a decision about a person does not go out automatically at all. I describe this tiering in more detail in the article on [human-in-the-loop AI](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/human-in-the-loop-ai).

#### 7. Errors are measured, not just retold

The pilot measures how often drafts are rewritten or discarded, how often the system abstains, and which questions lead to wrong answers. That list is the most valuable document in the project. It shows which sources are missing or out of date, and it is the evidence you put in front of management and data protection to show that the review works.

### What this means for choosing a model

“Which AI hallucinates the least?” is a common question, and the answer changes with every model generation. For a business product it is secondary. A mediocre model with clean sources, visible evidence and human review is more reliable than the best model answering freely from memory. The model can be swapped later. The sources, the interface and the workflow stay.

The same logic applies when you compare vendors: ask how the product behaves when the model is wrong, not which model is inside. I cover those questions in [what to prepare before hiring an AI integration partner](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/before-hiring-an-ai-integration-partner).

### What the EU AI Act says about it

The EU AI Act does not require error-free AI. For high-risk systems it requires human oversight (Article 14), and for AI that interacts with people it requires transparency (Article 50, which applies from 2 August 2026). The patterns above are the design answer to both requirements. This is a product designer’s reading, not legal advice.

### Where to start

The question is not whether your AI hallucinates. It does. The question is whether your product is built so that a wrong answer gets noticed before it takes effect. If you are planning an AI feature, or want an existing one reviewed, I can tell you in one conversation which of the seven patterns is missing first in your case: [get in touch](https://www.barnanorbert.com/contact). The method is described on the [AI integration](https://www.barnanorbert.com/ai-integration) page.

### Frequently asked questions

#### What does it mean when an AI hallucinates?

The model produces an output that sounds plausible but is wrong or backed by no source: an invented quote, a policy that does not exist, a wrong number. The model is not “lying”. It has no concept of true and false, only of likely.

#### Can you completely prevent AI hallucinations?

No. You can reduce them considerably by having the AI work from your sources and abstain when no source exists, and you can contain their effect by having a person review the output before it takes effect. A vendor who promises you hallucination-free AI is describing the product inaccurately.

#### Does RAG stop LLM hallucinations?

It helps against invented facts. It does not help against wrong summaries of the passages it found, against outdated documents or against mixed-up cases. That is why RAG always comes with visible sources and a review step.

#### Who is liable when a company’s AI gives a wrong answer?

The company that uses the output or passes it on to customers, not the model provider. That is exactly why human approval on consequential outputs is not mere caution: it is the place where the responsibility sits. The precise liability position is a question for your legal counsel.

#### Which AI model has the fewest hallucinations?

That changes with every model generation, and for your use case only a measurement on your own documents counts. In the prototype we test several models on the same examples and choose on that basis, not from a leaderboard.

#### Do you work with companies in Germany and the rest of the EU?

Yes. I work with companies in Hungary, Germany and the rest of the EU. Communication is in English or Hungarian; German-speaking teams work with me in English.
