## EU AI Act Article 50: what product teams must label now

- URL: https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/eu-ai-act-transparency-obligations
- Language: English
- Published: 2026-11-12; updated: 2026-11-12
- Author: Norbert Barna (https://www.linkedin.com/in/barna-norbert/)
- Also available in German: https://www.barnanorbert.com/de/wissen/ki-kennzeichnungspflicht; Hungarian: https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/irasok/ai-act-jelolesi-kotelezettseg
- Summary: EU AI Act Article 50 in practice: what has applied since August 2026, what the Digital Omnibus changed, and how to design the label.

The transparency obligations in Article 50 of the EU AI Act have applied since 2 August 2026. In short: if you run an AI system that interacts directly with people, you must tell those people, unless it is obvious from the circumstances. If you generate or publish AI-generated content, you must label it in certain cases, in particular deepfakes and machine-generated content. The 2026 Digital Omnibus moved many of the regulation’s deadlines, but not these duties.

I wrote this article for product teams, not for lawyers. It describes what the text asks for as I read it as a product lead, and above all how to design the disclosure so that it builds trust instead of being ignored like a warning sticker. It is not legal advice; which duty applies to your product is a question for your counsel.

On working together: I work with teams across the EU, and the work runs in English or Hungarian.

### What does Article 50 of the EU AI Act require?

Article 50 contains several transparency obligations for providers and deployers of certain AI systems. The AI disclosure requirements and the AI labelling requirements that people ask about are two sides of the same article. Read as a product team, it comes down to four cases:

1. **Interaction with people.** An AI system intended to interact directly with people (a customer service chatbot, for example) must be designed so that the person learns they are interacting with an AI, unless this is obvious to a reasonable person from the circumstances.
2. **Synthetic content.** Systems that artificially generate audio, image, video or text must mark their outputs in a machine-readable form, so that they can be recognised as artificially generated or manipulated.
3. **Deepfakes.** Anyone who generates or alters image, audio or video content that deceptively resembles real people, places or events must disclose that it was artificially generated or manipulated.
4. **Published AI text.** Anyone who publishes AI-generated text to inform the public on matters of public interest must disclose that, unless a person has reviewed the text and someone holds editorial responsibility for it.

These duties have applied since 2 August 2026. The Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026, in force since 27 July 2026) moved the obligations for high-risk systems under Annex III to 2 December 2027 and under Annex I to 2 August 2028, and it softened the AI literacy duty from “ensure” to “promote”. The transparency obligations in Article 50 stayed as they were (sources: [Cooley](https://cdp.cooley.com/digital-ai-omnibus-delays-key-deadlines-introduces-new-rules/), [National Law Review](https://natlawreview.com/article/eu-digital-omnibus-ai-enters-force), accessed 21 October 2026).

Two limits on this summary. For the exact exceptions, such as purposes authorised by law or content that is obviously artistic, the text of the regulation counts, not this article. And whether your system also falls under the high-risk rules is a separate question with its own timetable.

### Why the label is a design task

A sentence like “This answer was generated by AI” may satisfy the duty on paper. Whether it achieves anything depends on whether the person reads it, understands it and makes a better decision because of it.

At Instructure I led feature design for AI features in a learning platform that several million people used every day. Clear AI labelling was a guardrail there from day one, long before the regulation applied. The reason was not the law. Education, government and healthcare customers buy trust, and a label that says honestly what the AI did was part of that trust. The project is written up in the [Instructure case study](https://www.barnanorbert.com/work/instructure).

What we learned there fits into five decisions.

### Five decisions on AI labelling

#### 1. Where the label sits, and whether it stays

The label belongs on the output, not in the footer and not in the terms of use. Decide as well what happens when a person edits the output. Does the label disappear, does it become “suggested by AI, edited by a person”, or does it stay unchanged? Each of those answers can be defended. Having no answer is the problem.

#### 2. What the label says

“AI-generated” says very little. It is more useful to say what the AI did: summarised, translated, wrote a draft, calculated a recommendation. At Instructure the principle was “explanation before suggestion”: the signals and sources behind a suggestion came before the suggestion itself. That is labelling that helps a person decide.

#### 3. The moment of disclosure in a conversation

In customer service the notice belongs at the start of the conversation, not in the third reply, and it should be repeated when a person takes over. At every point the customer should know whether they are talking to an AI or to a person, and how to reach a person.

#### 4. Labelling and human review belong together

An output that is labelled as AI-generated but can be neither edited nor rejected produces distrust, not trust. At Instructure every AI suggestion had a label, an edit state and a way back, and nothing the model decided was allowed to stay invisible. I describe the patterns behind this in [human-in-the-loop AI for regulated products](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/human-in-the-loop-ai).

#### 5. What gets logged

For the duty to mark synthetic content in a machine-readable form, and for later reviews, it must be possible to trace which output was generated by which system and who edited it. That is a decision about the data model and the logging. Make it before you build, not after the first request from a supervisory authority.

### What this means for small and mid-sized companies

Most small and mid-sized companies are affected by Article 50 in exactly one of two ways: they use an AI system that talks to customers, or they publish AI-generated content. Both can be handled with the five decisions above inside a pilot project, without building a legal department.

What matters is bringing legal advice in early. At Instructure, Legal, Compliance and Data Science co-wrote the guardrails from the start. They did not inspect them at the end.

A checklist to begin with:

- Which of our AI features interact directly with people?
- Which of them generate text, image, audio or video that gets published?
- Where and when does the person learn that AI is involved?
- Can the person edit the output, reject it or reach a human?
- What is logged, and who can stop the feature?

If you are about to bring in outside help for this, [what to prepare before hiring an AI integration partner](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/before-hiring-an-ai-integration-partner) lists the inputs worth having ready.

### Where to start

For a well-designed product the Article 50 duties are not an extra burden. They are the legal form of something users expect anyway: to know what they are dealing with. If you design the label, the edit state and the way back from the beginning, you meet the duty along the way.

If you are planning an AI feature that talks to customers, bring the workflow and [we start there](https://www.barnanorbert.com/contact). The method behind it is on the [AI integration](https://www.barnanorbert.com/ai-integration) page.

### Frequently asked questions

#### When do the EU AI Act transparency obligations apply?

The transparency obligations in Article 50 have applied since 2 August 2026. The 2026 Digital Omnibus did not postpone them.

#### Does every chatbot have to say it is an AI?

An AI system intended to interact directly with people must inform those people, unless it is obvious from the circumstances. Whether that exception covers your case is a question for your counsel.

#### Does Article 50 apply to AI tools used only internally?

Article 50 is aimed at interaction with people and at published content. An internal assistant whose outputs are checked by employees before anything goes out is a different case, and what an employer owes its own staff is a separate question. This is not legal advice.

#### What did the 2026 Digital Omnibus change in the AI Act?

It moved the deadlines for high-risk systems, Annex III to 2 December 2027 and Annex I to 2 August 2028, and it softened the AI literacy duty. The labelling and transparency obligations in Article 50 remained in place.

#### Is a notice in the terms of use enough for AI disclosure?

From a product point of view, no. The duty is aimed at the person being informed at the moment of interaction. Whether a specific implementation is legally sufficient is a question for your counsel; as a design matter the label belongs on the output.

#### Does AI-generated text have to be labelled?

Systems that generate text must mark their outputs in a machine-readable form. A visible disclosure is required when AI-generated text is published to inform the public on matters of public interest, unless a person has reviewed it and someone holds editorial responsibility. For the exact scope and exceptions, the text of the regulation counts.

---

## How much does a website cost? What the price depends on

- URL: https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/how-much-does-a-business-website-cost
- Language: English
- Published: 2026-11-12; updated: 2026-11-12
- Author: Norbert Barna (https://www.linkedin.com/in/barna-norbert/)
- Also available in Hungarian: https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/irasok/ceges-weboldal-ara; German: https://www.barnanorbert.com/de/wissen/was-kostet-eine-website
- Summary: How much does a website cost for a business? The nine factors behind the price, a real example and the questions to ask before a quote.

How much does a website cost? It depends on what the website has to do: who it is for, what a visitor should do on it, and which systems it connects to. Two quotes for the same request can differ many times over, and often both are fair, because they do not price the same work. I treat every website as custom work: technology, structure, design and content follow from what your users need, and so does the price.

There are no numbers in this article. I go through the nine factors that move the price of a custom business website the most, show an example from my own work, and describe how to ask for a quote you can compare with another.

### Why I don’t put a fixed price on a website

I believe in quality, not volume. A website from me is not a filled-in template. It is work that shows your brand, your products and my craft as they really are. So the price follows from what has to be built, not from the number of pages.

I work on projects where the client puts energy in as well: provides content, decides, gives feedback. A custom website is joint work. If you need a quickly filled template, that can be a good decision, but then I am not the best partner for it, and I say so in the first conversation.

### Why you get very different quotes for the same request

Two quotes rarely price the same thing. One sets up a template with your copy. The other starts with discovery, plans the visitor’s path, and builds the system that goes with it. Both are sold as “web development services”. The question is not which one is cheaper, but what is in the price. If neither says what the site has to achieve, they probably describe two different websites.

### What does the price of a business website depend on? Nine factors

#### 1. What the site has to achieve

A brochure site proves that the company exists and can be trusted. A lead generation site has to be found by people searching for your service, and has to lead them to get in touch. An online shop handles products, stock and payment. A web application is something users log into and work in. Each of the four is a different job.

#### 2. Content: who writes it, and how much there is

Copy and photos are often more work than the code. Finished copy just gets built in. Copy that has to be written or rewritten is skilled work: an interview with you, understanding the offer, editing, rounds of approval. A second language is not a translate button: every page exists twice, with its own title, description and search optimisation.

#### 3. Custom design or a template

A ready-made template launches fast, and for many companies it is enough. Custom design pays off when visitors need to trust you before they decide, or when the content does not fit a template’s structure. It is more than the look: it covers navigation, the mobile view, forms and error states.

#### 4. Features and integrations

Every feature that talks to another system brings its own work and its own failure cases. A contact form needs a decision on where the message goes and how spam is filtered. Online payment needs the successful, the failed and the abandoned payment handled. A member area needs login, permissions, and paid content that really stays protected. CRM, invoicing, newsletter, booking calendar: wherever data moves, the error handling has to be designed too.

#### 5. Technology that fits your users

A static site, a site on a content management system, or a web application: the choice comes from what your visitors and your team need, not from habit. In my [web development work](https://www.barnanorbert.com/web-development) the technology is fitted to the users too. A brochure site that rarely changes does not need the system a paid membership platform needs, and a web application should not be forced into a site builder.

#### 6. Content management after launch

Who changes the site after launch? If it rarely changes, the developer can make the edits. If new articles, offers or courses appear regularly, you need a content management system your team works in without a developer, and will actually use. Ask to be shown it before handover.

#### 7. Privacy and security

If the site measures visits, the GDPR requires the visitor’s consent, and the measurement has to stay off until the visitor has decided. You need a privacy notice, and a form has to say where the data goes. For health or financial topics the bar is higher: security has to live in the code, for example as a strict content security policy, not on a policy page.

#### 8. Accessibility, findability, speed

The European Accessibility Act, Directive (EU) 2019/882, has applied since 28 June 2025 to certain services, for example e-commerce. Microenterprises providing services are exempt. Whether it applies to you is a question for a lawyer. This is a product designer’s reading, not legal advice. Keyboard navigation and sufficient contrast belong to a good site either way.

A finished site does not appear in Google by itself. Fast loading, server-side rendering, a unique title and description per page, structured data, a sitemap and marked-up language versions are cheap while building and expensive afterwards. Ask what the quote means by search optimisation: the technical foundations, or keyword research and a content plan as well. Those are two different jobs.

#### 9. Operations, maintenance, deadline

The price does not end at launch. There are domain and hosting fees, the content management system and its dependencies need updates, backups have to exist, and someone has to notice when something goes down. A tight launch date rearranges the work: shorter feedback rounds, and often some features move to a second round.

### An example: what went into the Kineticare platform

Two physiotherapists who specialise in hand and arm rehabilitation wanted to bring the same method to patients who will never sit in their treatment room. I designed and built it: brand, content, interface, a Next.js platform, Payload as the content management system (the physiotherapists publish without a developer), course videos streamed from a CDN, Barion payment, a member area for paid content, GDPR consent management and a strict content security policy.

The lesson for the price: the “website” here was in fact a product. The work was in the patient journey, the payment and the member access, not in the number of pages. The details are in the [Kineticare case study](https://www.barnanorbert.com/work/kineticare).

### How to ask for a quote on a custom website

1. Describe in one paragraph who the site is for and what a visitor should do on it: call, pay, sign up.
2. List the features using the factors above, and mark what is needed for launch and what can wait.
3. Write down the systems you already have: invoicing, CRM, booking calendar, newsletter tool.
4. Decide who writes the copy and who manages the site after launch.
5. Ask for a quote that states, item by item, what is included, what is not, and how maintenance works.

Then put the same questions to everyone who quotes, [me included](https://www.barnanorbert.com/contact):

- What is the goal of the site, and what counts as success?
- Are copywriting, photography and translation included?
- Template or custom design? How many design rounds?
- Who changes the site after launch, and how?
- Which integrations are included, and what happens when an external service does not respond?
- What does the search optimisation cover?
- What does running the site cost per month or per year, and who is responsible when something breaks?
- Who owns the source code, the domain and the content?

### What is usually not included in the price of a website?

In my experience, ongoing content production, paid advertising, photography (unless stated separately) and third-party fees such as hosting, the domain, the payment provider’s commission and the email system are usually not part of the price. This is an observation, not market data, so always ask.

### Where to start

The price of a website is a consequence of what you expect from it. If you want it to bring in clients and show your brand as it really is, then content, trust and measurement are part of the work. Say that in the first conversation. Once the five steps are written down, [send them over](https://www.barnanorbert.com/contact) and I will tell you what you need for launch.

### Frequently asked questions

#### How much does a website cost for a small business?

The range is wide, because the word “website” does not describe the same work every time. Every website I build is custom work, so the price follows from the task: the content, the features, the integrations and the maintenance. With the five steps above written down, I can give you a precise quote, and you can compare two quotes for the same work.

#### Is a website built from a template cheaper?

At launch, usually yes. Customisation and later extensions can make it more expensive if the template’s structure does not fit your visitors. For many companies a ready-made template is enough.

#### How long does it take to build a website?

It depends mostly on the content and the number of features, not on the code. Once the scope is itemised I can name a date. I don’t promise a general number of weeks.

#### What is the difference between a website and a web application?

Once it includes login, payment or data processing, it is an application. That needs different design, testing and operations. I write more about it on the [web development](https://www.barnanorbert.com/web-development) page.

#### Does my business website have to be accessible?

The European Accessibility Act has applied to certain services since June 2025, and microenterprises providing services are exempt. Whether it applies to you is a question for your lawyer. Keyboard use and good contrast are part of a good site regardless.

#### Do you work with companies outside Hungary?

Yes. I work with clients in Hungary, Germany and other EU countries. The work runs in English or Hungarian.

## MVP development for regulated products: what must be real

- URL: https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/mvp-development-regulated-products
- Language: English
- Published: 2026-11-12; updated: 2026-11-28
- Author: Norbert Barna (https://www.linkedin.com/in/barna-norbert/)
- Also available in German: https://www.barnanorbert.com/de/wissen/mvp-entwicklung-regulierte-produkte; Hungarian: https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/irasok/mvp-fejlesztes-szabalyozott-termekhez
- Summary: MVP development for fintech, health and other regulated markets: what you can leave out, what must be real on day one, and how.

An MVP, a minimum viable product, is the smallest version of a product that lets you test one central assumption with real users. In MVP development for a regulated market, such as payments, health, insurance or gambling, the principle is the same, with one restriction: what you may leave out is scope. What you may not leave out is everything that concerns trust and permissibility: identity verification, consent, data protection, secure confirmation of consequential actions, traceability. Those are real on day one, or the product does not go to real users.

This article describes how building an MVP for regulated industries differs from the startup textbook, what had to be real on day one in projects I worked on, and what the process looks like from hypothesis to first user. I work with companies across the EU; the work runs in English or Hungarian.

### In short: an MVP for a regulated market

- **Definition:** an MVP, a minimum viable product, is the smallest version of a product that lets you test one central assumption with real users.
- **The rule:** you may cut scope. You may not cut identity verification, consent, data protection, confirmation of consequential actions or traceability. A facade is allowed, a fake foundation is not.
- **Prototype or MVP:** a prototype is not functional and does not go to real users; an MVP is functional and does. In a regulated product the prototype comes first, because the critical flows can be tested before any duties apply.
- **AI in the MVP:** if users interact with an AI system, the AI Act’s transparency rules (Article 50) apply from 2 August 2026, to an MVP as well. The European Commission lists credit scoring among the high-risk use cases, whose rules apply from 2 December 2027.
- **What sets the duration:** the duty list and the integrations, such as identity verification and payment, more than the features.

### What is an MVP, and what can it not be in a regulated market?

The lean startup idea behind the MVP is build, measure, learn, in short loops, with as little effort as possible. A landing page, a clickable dummy or a facade operated by hand is often enough to find out whether anyone wants the product.

Regulated markets set two limits on that.

The first is legal. As soon as real users bring real money, real health data or real identities, duties apply that no MVP status suspends: the General Data Protection Regulation, payment services rules such as PSD2 with strong customer authentication, anti-money-laundering rules with identity verification and, depending on the product, the AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (source: [EUR-Lex, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), accessed 22 October 2026).

The second is about what you are measuring. In these markets trust is the assumption under test. A fintech MVP that feels unsafe at the moment a payment is confirmed does not tell you whether the idea is good. It only tells you that users do not trust the product.

That gives the split this article proposes: **a facade is allowed, a fake foundation is not.**

### What you can leave out

- Secondary features that are not part of the central assumption: settings, exports, statistics, multiple languages.
- Automation behind the scenes. Much of what a system will do later can be done by a person in the MVP, as long as the user does not notice and no duty is breached.
- Scale. An MVP has to carry a hundred users, not a hundred thousand.
- Polish in the design. Clear and consistent, yes. Refined, no.

None of this is a compromise on quality. It is the point of an MVP: every feature you do not build is a week you spend learning instead.

### What must be real on day one

#### 1. Identity and consent

Whoever signs up has to be who they say they are, where the product requires it, and has to know what they are consenting to. At Benker, a banking platform on blockchain infrastructure, I was responsible for the entire entry into the product: onboarding, the KYC check, card linking with 3DS confirmation. None of it was a placeholder in the MVP. The work was to design the mandatory steps so that people who had never opened a bank account in an app understood them and got through: clear guidance, visible progress, errors explained, a way back. Details: [Benker case study](https://www.barnanorbert.com/work/benker).

#### 2. Confirmation of consequential actions

Deposit, execute, withdraw. Each of these actions needs a confirmation that shows what will happen, what it costs and whether it can be undone. At Benker we introduced one consistent presentation for every state, open, pending, successful, failed, escalated, so that the product behaves the same way everywhere. That sounds like polish. It is foundation: a user who does not know whether their transfer is on its way calls support or leaves.

#### 3. Data protection in the code, not in the policy

Consent before tracking, data minimisation, encrypted transport, a strict Content Security Policy. On Kineticare, a health platform I designed and built, analytics tools stay off until the visitor agrees, and the application ships with a strict security policy. A health product carries more data protection risk than a portfolio site, and that has to be right in the code, not on a page of legal text. Details: [Kineticare case study](https://www.barnanorbert.com/work/kineticare).

#### 4. Traceability

Who approved what and when, which version of the terms the user accepted, which decision a system made. These records cannot be produced after the fact. In the MVP they can be simple, but they have to be complete from the start.

#### 5. With AI: labelling, review, confidence

At SportsGambit, an AI-supported prediction-market MVP, every recommendation carried a confidence score and the agent’s track record, and a deliberate review step stood before any action. Early telemetry showed that users relied heavily on the AI suggestions, which we treated as a risk, not as a success. The AI Act names this tendency: Article 14(4)(b) asks that the people overseeing a high-risk system “remain aware of the possible tendency of automatically relying or over-relying on the output”, which it calls automation bias. The patterns behind this are described in [human-in-the-loop AI for regulated products](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/human-in-the-loop-ai).

The case study draws a clear boundary here. It describes the information architecture and the explainability of the MVP, and it does not claim that production-grade safeguards for real-money betting were shipped. Before a launch with real money, age and location checks, deposit and loss limits, self-exclusion options and a legal review would be launch requirements. Details: [SportsGambit case study](https://www.barnanorbert.com/work/sportsgambit).

### The process: from hypothesis to first user

1. **Name the one assumption.** What has to be true for the product to make sense? One sentence, measurable.
2. **Write the duty list.** Which rules apply the moment a real user arrives. Legal counsel co-writes this list, in the first week.
3. **Separate facade from foundation.** Everything that is neither the assumption nor a duty goes on the “leave out” or the “by hand” list. Everything else is built for real.
4. **Design the critical flows first.** Onboarding, confirmation, errors, the way back. Prototype, test with users and revise before a line of product code is written.
5. **Build in short loops,** with measurement from the start: where users drop off, where they call, where they hesitate.
6. **Launch with a few real users,** behind restricted access, with one named owner who reads the numbers every week.
7. **Decide.** Extend, rebuild or stop, based on what users did, not on what they said.

The order matters. Step two comes before any design work because the duty list decides how much of the product is foundation and how much can stay facade.

: MVP development for a regulated product: what is ready at the end of each phase, and who must take part
| Phase | Ready at the end | Who must take part |
|---|---|---|
| Assumption and duty list (steps 1 and 2) | One measurable assumption; a written list of the rules that apply once a real user arrives | Founder or product owner, legal counsel |
| Facade and foundation (step 3) | Three lists: leave out, do by hand, build for real | Product owner, designer, lead developer |
| Critical flows (step 4) | A prototype of onboarding, confirmation, errors and the way back, tested with users and revised | Designer, test users, whoever reviews compliance |
| Build (step 5) | A working product with real identity checks, consent, confirmations and records; measurement switched on | Developers, designer, the identity and payment providers |
| Restricted launch (step 6) | A few real users behind restricted access; numbers read every week | One named owner, support |
| Decision (step 7) | A documented decision: extend, rebuild or stop | Product owner and whoever funds the next stage |

### Who builds an MVP for a regulated market?

A small team builds it: one person who owns the product decisions, a designer for the critical flows, one or more developers, and legal counsel who co-writes the duty list. Identity verification and payment are usually connected from specialised providers, not built from scratch. I cover the product design and the web development; the legal review stays with your counsel.

### What is ready at the end of an MVP?

At the end of an MVP you have a working product in the hands of a few real users, complete records of who consented to and approved what, and measurements of where users dropped off or hesitated. You also have a decision on the one assumption: extend, rebuild or stop. What you do not have yet is scale, secondary features or refined design.

### What effort and cost depend on when you commission an MVP

- Which duties apply: identity verification, payment processing, health data, AI labelling.
- Whether payments or third-party systems are integrated.
- How much of the foundation already exists, for example a design system or a component library.
- The number of platforms: web, iOS, Android.
- How many users the launch has to carry.

I do not quote a fixed price, because every project is individual work; the price follows once the duty list and the one assumption are settled. How I approach this kind of SaaS development and product work is described on the [web development and product design](https://www.barnanorbert.com/web-development) page.

### Where to start

An MVP in a regulated market is small in scope and complete in its foundation. That holds with or without AI, for a web application as much as for a mobile app. Tell me your one assumption and the market the product launches in, and in one conversation I will tell you what belongs on the duty list and what you can safely leave out: [get in touch](https://www.barnanorbert.com/contact).

### Sources

- [AI Act](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai), European Commission, Shaping Europe’s digital future, accessed 28 November 2026
- [Article 14: Human oversight](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-14), AI Act Service Desk, European Commission, accessed 28 November 2026

### Frequently asked questions

#### What does the MVP approach mean?

It means building the smallest version of a product that lets you test one central assumption with real users, and then learning from what those users do before you build more. The approach comes from the lean startup method.

#### How long does MVP development take?

In regulated markets, a few weeks to a few months, depending on the duty list and the integrations. The mandatory steps, such as identity verification and payment, determine the duration more than the actual features do.

#### What is the difference between a prototype and an MVP?

A prototype tests whether people understand a flow; it is not functional and does not go to real users. An MVP is functional, goes to real users and tests whether they use it. In regulated products the prototype comes before the MVP, because it lets you test the critical flows before any duties apply.

#### Can you build an MVP with no-code tools?

For the facade, yes. For identity verification, payment, data protection and logging, only if the platform demonstrably meets those requirements. That has to be checked before the launch, not after it.

#### Does the EU AI Act apply to an AI MVP?

If users interact with an AI, the Article 50 transparency duty has applied since 2 August 2026, and it applies to an MVP too. High-risk obligations, for example for credit decisions, apply from 2 December 2027 following the 2026 Digital Omnibus. This is a product team’s reading, not legal advice.

#### What must a fintech MVP include from day one?

Everything that concerns trust and permissibility: identity verification and consent, a clear confirmation for every consequential action, data protection built into the code, and complete records of who approved what. Features can wait. These cannot, because without them the product may not go to real users at all.

---

## What to prepare before hiring an AI integration partner

- URL: https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/before-hiring-an-ai-integration-partner
- Language: English
- Published: 2026-10-21; updated: 2026-11-28
- Author: Norbert Barna (https://www.linkedin.com/in/barna-norbert/)
- Also available in Hungarian: https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/irasok/ai-fejleszto-partner-valasztasa; German: https://www.barnanorbert.com/de/wissen/ki-dienstleister-auswaehlen
- Summary: What to prepare before hiring an AI integration partner: one workflow, a baseline, data access, what stays human, and a pilot owner.

Before you hire an AI integration partner, prepare five things: one workflow described by the people who do it, a baseline of how it performs today, the data and systems the AI may touch, the decisions a person must keep, and the measure that would make a pilot worth continuing. With those, a first conversation produces a scoped proposal instead of a demo.

This article is the preparation checklist I wish every company brought to the first call, the questions worth asking any partner, and the red flags I would watch for. The tone is practical; the pitch, such as it is, comes at the end.

### In short: what to prepare before hiring an AI integration partner

- **Bring five things:** one workflow described by the people who do it, a baseline, the data and systems the AI may touch, the decisions a person keeps, and the measure that decides whether a pilot continues.
- **A baseline is:** time per case, error rate and waiting time, taken from your own records before any partner is hired.
- **Do not share yet:** passwords, customer data or confidential material. An anonymised one-page description of the workflow is enough for a first conversation.
- **A good first conversation ends with:** a bounded problem, a draft of access and review rules, a decision on whether to prototype, and a statement of what the prototype must prove.
- **Why outside help is common:** in 2025, 19.95% of EU enterprises used AI technologies, and among enterprises that considered AI but did not use it, lack of relevant expertise was the reason given most often (70.89%), ahead of unclear legal consequences (52.52%) (Eurostat, data extracted December 2025).

### Why does preparation change the quality of proposals?

Without a workflow and a baseline, a partner can only show you what a model can do, and every partner’s model can do roughly the same things. With them, the partner has to say what will change in your work, how, and how you will know. That is a different conversation, and it separates an AI integration consultant who puts AI into real operations from people who sell demos. The same holds whether the offer is called AI consulting, AI implementation or AI integration services: the names differ, the test is the same. This is an editorial view from my own projects, not a market figure.

### The preparation checklist

#### 1. One workflow, described by the people who do it

Pick one repeated task and have the people who do it describe the inputs, the hand-offs, the decisions they make again and again, and what a mistake costs. This mirrors the first step of my own method: map the work before the solution.

Be ready for the honest answer that the task needs simpler rules or a clearer interface rather than AI. A good partner says so in the first meeting.

#### 2. A baseline

Time per case, error rate, waiting time, from your own records. If you have none, that is the first task, and it is worth doing before any partner is hired, because without it nobody can tell you later whether the pilot helped.

#### 3. Data and access

Which systems hold the data, which data is approved for use, where information may go, and who approves access. Do not send passwords, customer data or confidential material to anyone before a sharing method is agreed. An anonymised one-page description of the workflow is enough for a first conversation.

#### 4. What stays human

What may the AI suggest, what must a person check, and what happens on a missing or wrong answer. At Instructure, where I led end-to-end feature design for AI features in an enterprise learning platform, we started with what must stay human, not with what could be automated. The interface patterns that came out of that are in [Human-in-the-loop AI for regulated products](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/human-in-the-loop-ai).

#### 5. A success measure and an owner

Which measure decides whether the pilot continues: task completion, review effort, output quality, response time or running cost, compared with your baseline. And one named person on your side who can pause the pilot or roll it back. In my method that owner exists from the pilot’s first day.

#### 6. Your constraints

Languages, regulated data, accessibility requirements, procurement rules, and your exposure to the EU AI Act. For orientation: the Article 50 transparency duties apply from 2 August 2026, and after the Digital Omnibus (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744) the Annex III high-risk obligations apply from 2 December 2027, dates the European Commission’s AI Act page confirms (sources: [Cooley](https://cdp.cooley.com/digital-ai-omnibus-delays-key-deadlines-introduces-new-rules/), [National Law Review](https://natlawreview.com/article/eu-digital-omnibus-ai-enters-force), accessed 2026-10-21). Not legal advice; which category your system falls into is a question for your counsel.

### Questions to ask an AI integration partner

1. What would you test before building anything?
2. How do you evaluate output quality on our own examples?
3. What happens in the interface when the output is wrong, empty or late?
4. Who on your side builds, and who on ours owns it after hand-over?
5. How do we stop or roll back the pilot?
6. What will you not do? Ask for a clear “not in scope” list.
7. Which of your past projects is closest to ours, and what exactly was your role in it?
8. How do you handle our data during the prototype?

: Questions to ask an AI integration partner: what a good answer contains and what should warn you
| Question to ask | A good answer | A warning sign |
|---|---|---|
| What would you test before building anything? | Names your workflow, representative examples and what the prototype must prove | A demo before any question about your workflow |
| How do you evaluate quality on our own examples? | A set of your cases with expected results, compared with your baseline | Success promised before a baseline exists |
| What happens when the output is wrong, empty or late? | Describes the review step, the failure states and the way back | No answer on failure states |
| Who owns it after hand-over, and how do we stop it? | A named owner on your side who can pause the pilot or roll it back | No named owner after hand-over |
| What will you not do? | A written “not in scope” list | A proposal that names a model before it names your task |
| Which past project is closest, and what was your role? | Role and boundaries stated, including what was not shipped | A logo list with no role named |
| How do you handle our data during the prototype? | Approved, anonymised examples and an agreed sharing method | A request for passwords or raw customer data up front |

Question seven is the one most portfolios answer vaguely. Mine states role and boundaries on every case page, including what was not shipped, because that is the information you need to compare partners.

### Red flags

These are opinions from experience, not rules.

- A demo before any question about your workflow.
- No answer on failure states.
- Success promised before a baseline exists.
- No named owner after hand-over.
- A proposal that names a model before it names your task.

### Who should be in the first conversation from your side?

Three roles are enough: the person who owns the workflow and can decide, someone who does the task every day and can describe its inputs and exceptions, and whoever approves access to the systems and data. If the workflow touches customers or regulated data, add your compliance contact or counsel early. A first call with only a sponsor and no one who does the work usually ends with a demo request.

### What I look for in a project

I believe in quality over volume. I take on a small number of projects where the client puts in energy too, and where neither of us is aiming for a template, but for work that represents the client’s brand and product and my own craft. A company that prepares the checklist above is usually that client.

### What a good first conversation produces

A bounded problem. A draft of access and review rules. A decision on whether to prototype. And a statement of what the prototype must prove before anyone builds. Those are the deliverables of the first three steps of my [AI integration method](https://www.barnanorbert.com/ai-integration#workflow); the prototype itself comes before any development commitment.

### Frequently asked questions

#### What does an AI integration partner do?

An AI integration consultant or partner connects AI to the workflow, data and decisions you already have, designs the review and failure paths, and builds the pilot with your systems. The work is in the integration, not in the model.

#### How long does an AI integration take?

It depends on the workflow, the data and the number of systems involved. The prototype step exists to answer this before a build; I do not quote a fixed duration in advance.

#### Do we need our data cleaned first?

You need to know which data is approved and where it lives. The prototype shows what quality is enough for your task, which is usually less than people fear and more than a demo needs.

#### Should we hire a consultant or a development company?

Ask who builds and who owns it after hand-over. Some partners do both; I design the workflow and build the pilot, including the web platform if one is needed. The [Kineticare case study](https://www.barnanorbert.com/work/kineticare) shows the build side of that work.

#### Do you work with companies in Germany and the rest of the EU?

Yes. Communication is in English or Hungarian; German-speaking teams work with me in English.

#### What does it cost?

Every engagement is scoped to the workflow, the data and the integrations, so the price follows from that scope. There are no fixed packages, and I give a proposal after the first conversation, not before.

### Where to start

Bring the workflow, who uses it, the systems and data involved, and what success would look like. That is enough for a [first conversation](https://www.barnanorbert.com/contact), and it is the difference between a proposal and a demo.

### Sources

- [Use of artificial intelligence in enterprises](https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Use_of_artificial_intelligence_in_enterprises), Eurostat Statistics Explained, data extracted December 2025, accessed 28 November 2026
- [AI Act](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai), European Commission, Shaping Europe’s digital future, accessed 28 November 2026

## Human-in-the-loop AI for regulated products: 7 patterns

- URL: https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/human-in-the-loop-ai
- Language: English
- Published: 2026-10-21; updated: 2026-11-28
- Author: Norbert Barna (https://www.linkedin.com/in/barna-norbert/)
- Also available in German: https://www.barnanorbert.com/de/wissen/human-in-the-loop-ki; Hungarian: https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/irasok/human-in-the-loop-emberi-felugyelet
- Summary: Human-in-the-loop AI patterns that hold up in review: labels, editable outputs, source cues, failure states, a stop. From shipped work.

Human-in-the-loop AI means a person reviews, edits or approves what the system proposes before it has an effect, and can override or stop it. In a regulated product that is not a checkbox at the end of the project. It is a set of interface decisions made on day one: what the AI may suggest, what a person must check, how the person sees why, and what happens when the output is wrong.

This article describes seven patterns that held up in review in two products I worked on: AI features in Instructure’s learning platform, and an AI-based prediction-market MVP called SportsGambit. The examples come from those projects; the conclusions are mine.

### In short: human-in-the-loop AI in five facts

- **Definition:** human-in-the-loop AI is a workflow in which the system proposes and a person reviews, edits or approves each consequential output before it takes effect.
- **The test:** a person is in the loop only if three things hold: they can see that AI was involved, they can change or reject the output, and the decision is recorded.
- **The decision rule:** choose human in the loop when a wrong output would reach a customer, move money or affect a person’s rights. Human on the loop is enough only where an error is cheap and someone sees it afterwards.
- **The law:** Article 14 of the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) requires that high-risk AI systems can be “effectively overseen by natural persons” while in use, including the ability to override the output and to interrupt the system through a “stop” button or a similar procedure.
- **The dates:** according to the European Commission, the AI Act’s transparency rules apply from 2 August 2026, the rules for Annex III high-risk use cases from 2 December 2027, and those for high-risk systems embedded in regulated products (Annex I) from 2 August 2028.

### What does human-in-the-loop AI mean, and what does it not?

Three terms are commonly used, and they describe different amounts of human control:

- **Human in the loop:** a person approves each consequential output before it takes effect.
- **Human on the loop:** the system acts on its own; a person monitors and can intervene.
- **Human out of the loop:** fully automated, with review only after the fact, if at all.

These are design terms, not legal categories. In regulated industries the right level depends on the consequence of a wrong output, not on how good the model is. A draft that a person edits anyway can tolerate a weaker model; an action that reaches a customer or moves money cannot.

Three things have to be true for a person to be genuinely in the loop. They can see that the AI was involved. They can change or reject the output. And the decision is recorded, so that who accepted what, and on what basis, can be reconstructed later. If any one of these is missing, the person is not in the loop. They are watching it.

### What the EU AI Act asks of human oversight

Article 14 of the EU AI Act requires that high-risk AI systems be designed so the people overseeing them can understand the system’s capacities and limitations, remain aware of automation bias, interpret the output correctly, decide not to use it or override it, and stop it through a “stop” button or a similar procedure (source: [AI Act Service Desk, Article 14](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-14), accessed 2026-10-21).

On timing: the Digital Omnibus on AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026) moved the Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 and the Annex I obligations to 2 August 2028. The Article 50 transparency duties, such as telling people they are interacting with an AI system, still apply from 2 August 2026 (sources: [Cooley](https://cdp.cooley.com/digital-ai-omnibus-delays-key-deadlines-introduces-new-rules/), [National Law Review](https://natlawreview.com/article/eu-digital-omnibus-ai-enters-force), accessed 2026-10-21).

This is a design reading of the text, not legal advice. Whether your system is high-risk is a question for your counsel. What I can say from shipped work is that each of the five oversight abilities in Article 14 maps to an interface decision, and the rest of this article is those decisions.

: Article 14(4) of the EU AI Act: the five oversight abilities and the interface decision behind each
| Ability in Article 14(4) | Interface decision | Pattern below |
|---|---|---|
| (a) Understand capacities and limitations, monitor operation | Label every AI output; show the empty, late and error states | 1 and 4 |
| (b) Remain aware of automation bias | Show confidence and track record; keep a deliberate review step | 5 |
| (c) Interpret the output correctly | Show signals and sources before the suggestion | 2 |
| (d) Decide not to use, disregard, override or reverse the output | Editable, undoable outputs with draft, reviewed and published states | 3 |
| (e) Intervene or interrupt through a “stop” button or similar | Feature flag and a named owner who can pause or roll back | 7 |

### Seven human-in-the-loop AI patterns that hold up in review

#### 1. Label every AI output

At Instructure, where I led end-to-end feature design within the Canvas Catalog ecosystem, part of a product that several million people used every day, clear AI labelling and disclosure was a guardrail fixed on day one. Every AI suggestion had a label, an edit state and a way back, and nothing the model decided could remain invisible.

Decide before building: the wording of the label, where it sits, and whether it persists after a person has edited the output.

#### 2. Explain first, then suggest

The Instructure design principle was “explanation before suggestion”: show the signals and sources behind a suggestion before the suggestion itself. A reviewer who sees why can judge; a reviewer who only sees what can only trust.

Decide: which source cue the reviewer can actually verify in the time they have. A citation nobody opens is decoration.

#### 3. Make outputs editable and reversible

Outputs at Instructure were editable and undoable, with explicit review states: draft, reviewed, published. This is the interface form of Article 14’s “decide not to use, override or reverse”. An AI output that can only be accepted or rejected pushes people toward accepting.

#### 4. Design the states nobody demos

We shipped accessible component states for empty, loading, error and latency across every product variant. In a review, the failure state is where the questions start: what does the instructor see when the model returns nothing, returns late, or returns something it should not? If the interface hides those states, a person cannot review what they cannot see.

#### 5. Show confidence, and keep a deliberate review step

At SportsGambit, a prediction-market MVP with AI agents recommending picks, every tip carried a confidence score, leaderboards let users check an agent’s history before acting on its advice, and a deliberate review step stood before any action. Early product data showed heavy use of AI-originated recommendations; we treated that as a risk to watch, not as a success metric, because automation reliance is exactly the failure mode human oversight is meant to catch. This maps to Article 14’s automation-bias requirement.

The case study also states its boundary: the MVP did not validate production wagering safeguards. Details: [SportsGambit case study](https://www.barnanorbert.com/work/sportsgambit).

#### 6. Put legal, compliance and data science in the room early

At Instructure the flows were reviewed jointly with Legal, Compliance and Data Science, and then codified into reusable patterns: prompts, review states, confirmations, feedback loops. They did not stand in our way at the end; they co-wrote the guardrails from the start. A guardrail added after the design is usually a warning dialog nobody reads.

The same held in non-AI regulated work. At Raiffeisen, where I was Product Lead for the mobile banking redesign, PSD2, strong customer authentication, KYC and audit trail arrived as non-negotiables. We kept almost every step and changed how it felt to go through them. That is the regulated-delivery parallel, not an AI example. Details: [Raiffeisen case study](https://www.barnanorbert.com/work/raiffeisen).

#### 7. Ship behind flags, measure, and name who can stop it

Features at Instructure went out behind feature flags, and we measured adoption and task completion so that every iteration built on what the data showed. In my [AI integration work](https://www.barnanorbert.com/ai-integration) the same idea becomes step four of the method: a bounded pilot with a named owner who can pause it or roll back to the previous version.

Decide: who owns the stop, how fast it can happen, and what is logged for later review.

### What to decide before you build: eight questions

1. What is the consequence of a wrong output, and for whom?
2. What may the AI suggest, and what must a person approve?
3. What does the reviewer see to judge the output?
4. How does the reviewer edit, reject or reverse it?
5. What happens on empty, missing or late output?
6. Who can stop the feature, and how fast?
7. What is logged for later review?
8. Which measures decide whether the pilot continues?

If these questions do not have answers yet, that is where the AI product design work starts, and human oversight is its first deliverable. In my method the second step, before anything is built, is defining access and human control: what the AI can suggest, what a person must review, and what happens when an answer is missing or wrong. If you are comparing partners, [what to prepare before hiring an AI integration partner](https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/before-hiring-an-ai-integration-partner) lists the inputs that make that conversation useful.

### Who designs human oversight in an AI product?

Human oversight is designed by the product team, not added by a reviewer at the end: the person responsible for the interface, with legal, compliance and data science reviewing the flows from the start. Article 14(3) of the EU AI Act splits the measures in two: those the provider builds into the system before it goes on the market, and those the provider identifies for the deployer to carry out. So if you buy an AI component, ask the vendor which oversight measures are built in and which are left to you.

### What is ready at the end of the oversight design work?

Before any model is connected, the design work ends with written answers to the eight questions above: what the AI may suggest and what a person must approve, the wording and place of the AI label, the review states, the screens for empty, late and wrong output, the named person who can stop the feature, and the list of what is logged. That set is what legal and compliance review, and it is what the pilot is built from. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework, a voluntary framework released on 26 January 2023, asks for the same thing in other words: trustworthiness considered in the design, development, use and evaluation of an AI product.

### What made it hard

Most AI projects start with what can be automated. At Instructure we started with what must stay human. The hard part was ethical, not technical: designing for the AI being wrong, biased or misused, instead of pretending those cases would not occur. That does not make for an impressive slide deck. It makes for AI that real institutions can roll out to millions of people and still sleep at night. Details: [Instructure case study](https://www.barnanorbert.com/work/instructure).

### Frequently asked questions

#### What is human-in-the-loop AI?

A workflow in which the system proposes and a person decides at defined points, with enough information to decide well. The person can see the AI was involved, can change or reject the output, and the decision is recorded.

#### Does the EU AI Act require human in the loop?

Article 14 requires effective human oversight for high-risk systems, including the ability to override and to stop the system. It does not prescribe one interface pattern. Whether a system is high-risk is a legal question; this article is not legal advice.

#### When do the high-risk obligations apply?

After the 2026 Digital Omnibus: Annex III systems from 2 December 2027, Annex I systems from 2 August 2028. Article 50 transparency duties apply from 2 August 2026.

#### Does human review slow everything down?

It moves effort to where a mistake costs most. Measure review effort in the pilot: if reviewers approve everything in two seconds, the loop is not working; if review takes longer than the original task, the feature is not working either.

#### Can a small team do this?

Yes. The patterns are interface decisions, not infrastructure. Start with one workflow, one label, one edit state and one named owner.

#### What is automation bias?

The tendency to over-trust a system’s output. The design response is visible confidence, verifiable sources and a deliberate review step before any action.

#### Do you work with teams in Germany and the rest of the EU?

Yes. Communication is in English or Hungarian; German-speaking teams work with me in English.

### Where to start

Human-in-the-loop AI is easier to design than to retrofit. The product that passes review is the one where every AI output already had a label, an edit state and a way back. Bring the workflow and the decision you are worried about, and [we start there](https://www.barnanorbert.com/contact).

### Sources

- [Article 14: Human oversight](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-14), AI Act Service Desk, European Commission, accessed 28 November 2026
- [AI Act](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai), European Commission, Shaping Europe’s digital future, accessed 28 November 2026
- [AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework), National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), AI RMF 1.0 released 26 January 2023, accessed 28 November 2026

# Hungarian articles

## AI fejlesztés ára: mitől függ, és mit kérdezz előtte

- URL: https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/irasok/ai-fejlesztes-ara-mitol-fugg
- Language: Hungarian
- Published: 2026-11-27; updated: 2026-11-28
- Author: Norbert Barna (https://www.linkedin.com/in/barna-norbert/)
- Also available in English: https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/what-ai-integration-cost-depends-on; German: https://www.barnanorbert.com/de/wissen/ki-beratung-kosten
- Summary: AI fejlesztés ára: nyolc tényező, amely drágítja vagy olcsóbbá teszi, a szakaszolás, két ajánlat összevetése és a futó költségek.

Az AI fejlesztés ára elsősorban nem a modelltől függ, hanem attól, mekkora folyamatot érint, milyen állapotban vannak az adataid, hány rendszerhez kell kapcsolódni, és mennyi ellenőrzés kell ahhoz, hogy az eredményben meg lehessen bízni. Ugyanaz a modell egy válaszvázlatot író belső eszközben és egy ügyfelekkel beszélő, több rendszerbe író megoldásban egészen más munkát jelent. Az indulás után futó költségek is vannak: a modellhasználat, a figyelés és a források karbantartása.

Ebben a cikkben nem írok számokat, mert minden AI fejlesztés és AI integráció egyedi munka, és egy szám feladat nélkül félrevezet. Nyolc tényezőt veszek sorra, utána leírom, hogyan bontható szakaszokra a munka, hogyan vess össze két ajánlatot, és mely futó költségek maradnak ki sok ajánlatból.

### Röviden: mitől függ az AI fejlesztés ára

- **Nyolc tényező mozgatja az árat:** a folyamat terjedelme, az adatok állapota, az integrációk, az emberi ellenőrzés szintje, a kiértékelés, a kockázat és a szabályozás, a nyelvek száma, és az, hogy ki tartja karban a megoldást.
- **A modell a kisebb tétel:** a munka nagy része tervezés, adat-előkészítés, integráció, ellenőrző felület és kiértékelés, nem a modell bekötése.
- **Így indulsz a legkisebb kiadással:** egyetlen szűk folyamat, rendezett források, és olyan kapcsolat, amely csak olvas a rendszereidből.
- **Négy szakasz, négy döntési pont:** felmérés, prototípus, pilot, bevezetés és átadás. Mindegyik végén dönthetsz, hogy folytatod-e.
- **Három futó költség marad az indulás után:** a modellhasználat, a monitorozás és a források karbantartása. Ehhez jön a jóváhagyó kolléga munkaideje.
- **Szabály két ajánlat összevetéséhez:** ha az egyikből hiányzik a kiértékelés, az emberi ellenőrzés vagy a hibaágak kezelése, akkor az nem olcsóbb, hanem kisebb munkát áraz.

### Mitől függ az AI fejlesztés ára? Nyolc tényező

#### 1. A folyamat terjedelme

A folyamat terjedelme azt jelenti, hány lépést, embert és döntést érint a megoldás, és hány kivétel fordul elő benne. Egy lépés, például a beérkező megkeresések besorolása, jól körülhatárolható. Egy több lépésből álló, önállóan cselekvő ügynök minden lépésnél új hibalehetőséget hoz, és mindegyiket meg kell tervezni és tesztelni kell. A rendhagyó esetek felismerése és biztonságos kezelése sokszor több munka, mint a főág.

#### 2. Az adatok állapota

Rendezett, elérhető és naprakész forrásból gyorsabban lesz megbízható eredmény, mint szétszórt, szkennelt vagy egymásnak ellentmondó dokumentumokból. Ha a tudás csak a kollégák fejében van meg, az első feladat a leírása, és ez nem AI-munka, de nélküle nincs mire építeni. Ezen a tényezőn te magad tudsz a legtöbbet javítani, még az ajánlatkérés előtt.

#### 3. Integrációk

Minden rendszer, amelyhez a megoldás kapcsolódik (CRM, levelezés, számlázó, belső adatbázis), saját jogosultságkezelést és saját hibaeseteket hoz. Nagy a különbség az olvasó és az író kapcsolat között. Ha az AI csak olvas, egy hiba rossz javaslatot eredményez. Ha ír is, a hiba bekerül a rendszeredbe, ezért visszaállítás, naplózás és jóváhagyási lépés kell hozzá. A dokumentált interfész nélküli, régi rendszerek tovább drágítanak.

#### 4. Az emberi ellenőrzés szintje

Az emberi ellenőrzés szintje azt rögzíti, mit javasolhat az AI, mit hagy jóvá ember, és mi történik bizonytalan vagy hiányzó válasznál. Ez felület is: szerkeszthető kimenet, forrásmegjelölés, elvetés, átadás embernek. Az ellenőrző felület pénzbe kerül, de e nélkül a megoldás nem futhat élesben. A mintákat külön cikkben írtam le: [Human in the loop: hét minta](https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/irasok/human-in-the-loop-emberi-felugyelet).

#### 5. Kiértékelés

A kiértékelés az a munka, amellyel bizonyítható, hogy a megoldás jól működik: valódi esetekből összeállított példakészlet, elfogadási feltételek és mérés a kiinduló állapothoz képest. Minél drágább egy hiba, annál több példa és annál szigorúbb küszöb kell. Az az ajánlat, amelyben nincs kiértékelés, olcsóbbnak látszik, de a minőség kérdését az éles működésre hagyja, amikor a javítás a legdrágább.

#### 6. Kockázat és szabályozás

Személyes, egészségügyi vagy pénzügyi adatoknál több tervezés, jogosultságkezelés, naplózás és egyeztetés kell a jogásszal vagy az adatvédelmi felelőssel. Ha az AI ügyfelekkel beszél, a jelölés is feladat, erről az [AI Act jelölési kötelezettségéről szóló cikkben](https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/irasok/ai-act-jelolesi-kotelezettseg) írok. Ha emberekről szóló döntést készít elő, a jogi vizsgálat megelőzi a technikát. Ez tervezési szempont, nem jogi tanácsadás.

#### 7. Nyelvek

Minden nyelv külön tesztelést jelent, mert egy modell minősége nyelvenként eltérhet, és a szakszavakat, a megszólítást és a hangnemet nyelvenként kell ellenőrizni. A magyar és a német anyagokhoz olyan ellenőr kell, aki a nyelvet és a szakterületet is ismeri.

#### 8. Ki tartja karban az indulás után

Egy AI-megoldás az indulás után is változik: frissülnek a források, a szolgáltató lecseréli a modellverziót, új kivételek jelennek meg. Ha a csapatod átveszi a működtetést, ahhoz dokumentáció, működtetési útmutató és betanítás kell az átadáskor. Ha külső partner tartja karban, az folyamatos tétel. A legdrágább változat az, amikor a megoldásnak nincs gazdája.

: AI fejlesztés ára: nyolc tényező, és mi viszi lefelé vagy felfelé a költséget
| Tényező | Mitől olcsóbb | Mitől drágább |
|---|---|---|
| A folyamat terjedelme | egy lépés, kevés kivétel | több lépés, önálló cselekvés, sok kivétel |
| Az adatok állapota | rendezett, elérhető, leírt tudás | szétszórt, szkennelt, ellentmondó források |
| Integrációk | egy rendszer, csak olvasás | több rendszer, írás, régi interfész |
| Emberi ellenőrzés | belső használat, gyors jóváhagyás | ügyfél felé menő vagy nehezen javítható kimenet |
| Kiértékelés | olcsón javítható hiba, kis példakészlet | drága hiba, szigorú elfogadási feltételek |
| Kockázat és szabályozás | nincs személyes vagy érzékeny adat | egészségügyi, pénzügyi adat, emberekről szóló döntés |
| Nyelvek | egy nyelv | több nyelv, nyelvenkénti tesztelés |
| Karbantartás | kijelölt belső gazda, átadott útmutató | nincs gazda, gyakran változó források |

A táblázat a saját szerkesztett tapasztalatom, nem piaci adat.

### Hogyan bontható szakaszokra egy AI integráció költsége?

Egy AI integráció költsége szakaszolható, és minden szakasz végén dönthetsz a folytatásról.

1. **Felmérés.** A munkát végző emberekkel végigvesszük a bemeneteket, az átadásokat, a döntéseket és a hibák következményeit. Az eredmény egy körülhatárolt probléma és egy kiinduló érték, amelyhez később mérni lehet. A felmérés önmagában is döntést ad arról, megéri-e továbbmenni, és arról is, hogy kell-e egyáltalán AI. Hogy melyik folyamattal érdemes kezdeni, azt az [AI automatizálás: melyik folyamattal kezdj](https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/irasok/ai-automatizalas-melyik-folyamattal-kezdj) cikk írja le.
2. **Prototípus.** Jóváhagyott, valódi példákkal készül, integráció nélkül, a leendő felhasználók bevonásával. Itt derül ki olcsón, hogy az adatok és a modell együtt elég jó eredményt adnak-e.
3. **Pilot.** Körülhatárolt felhasználói körrel, a szükséges legkevesebb integrációval, kijelölt felelőssel fut, aki le is állíthatja. A pilot alatt mérjük a működési költséget is, így a szélesebb bevezetés előtt már tény, nem becslés.
4. **Bevezetés és átadás.** A javítások, a dokumentáció és a működtetés felelőseinek kijelölése után jön a szélesebb kör.

A lépéseket az [AI tanácsadás, automatizálás és fejlesztés](https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/ai-tanacsadas-fejlesztes) oldalon részletezem, a kkv-knak szóló menetrendet az [AI bevezetése KKV-nál: az első 90 nap](https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/irasok/ai-bevezetese-kkv-elso-90-nap) cikkben.

### Mi készül el az egyes szakaszok végére, és ki dolgozik rajta?

A felmérés végén körülhatárolt probléma és kiinduló érték van, ehhez a folyamatot végző munkatársak és a folyamat gazdája kell. A prototípus végén valódi példákon kipróbált munkafelület van, még integráció nélkül, és a leendő felhasználók mondanak róla véleményt. A pilot végén mért eredmény és mért működési költség van, egy kijelölt felelőssel, aki le is állíthatta volna. Az átadás végén a tiéd a kód, a promptok, az értékelési példák és a működtetési útmutató. A te oldaladon végig három ember idejével számolj: a folyamat gazdájáéval, egy vagy két munkatárséval, aki a munkát ma végzi, és azéval, aki a rendszerekhez hozzáférést ad.

### Mennyi ideig tart egy AI fejlesztés?

Az időtartam ugyanattól a nyolc tényezőtől függ, mint az ár, ezért heteket feladat nélkül ugyanúgy nem lehet mondani, mint összeget. Három dolog nyújtja meg leggyakrabban: a rendszerekhez való hozzáférés jóváhagyása, a szétszórt források rendbetétele és a jogi egyeztetés. Egy nagykereskedésnél, ahol a rendelések e-mailben érkeznek és a cikktörzs rendezett, a prototípus gyorsan eljut a pilotig. Egy biztosítási alkusznál, ahol ügyféladat és több biztosító rendszere érintett, a hozzáférés és az adatkezelés tisztázása viszi az idő nagyobb részét.

### Egy példa: mi volt a munka az Instructure AI-funkcióiban

Az Instructure-nél egy tanulási platform AI-funkcióinak tervezését vezettem. A védőkorlátokat az első napon rögzítettük: emberi ellenőrzés, egyértelmű AI-jelölés, szerkeszthető kimenetek, forrásjelzések és helyreállítási utak. A folyamatokat a jogi, a megfelelőségi és a data science csapattal közösen néztük át, és mértük a használatba vételt és a feladatok befejezését.

Az ár szempontjából két tanulság van. Az egyik: a felsorolt tételek mind tervezési, fejlesztési és egyeztetési munkát jelentenek, és egyik sem maga a modell. A másik: a megoldásokat újrahasznosítható mintákba foglaltuk (promptok, ellenőrzési állapotok, megerősítések, visszajelzési körök), így a következő funkció kész mintákra épülhetett. Egy cégnél ugyanez igaz: az első folyamat viseli az alapok költségét, a második már épít rájuk. A részletek az [Instructure esettanulmányban](https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/munka/instructure) olvashatók.

### Hogyan hasonlíts össze két AI fejlesztési ajánlatot?

Két AI fejlesztési ajánlat akkor hasonlítható össze, ha ugyanazt a terjedelmet árazza. Ezeket nézd meg mindkettőben:

- **Terjedelem:** melyik folyamatot, hány lépést és milyen kivételeket fed le, és mi marad ki kifejezetten.
- **Adat-előkészítés:** ki rendezi a forrásokat, és benne van-e az árban.
- **Integráció:** mely rendszerekhez kapcsolódik, olvas vagy ír is, és mi történik, ha egy rendszer nem válaszol.
- **Ellenőrzés:** van-e jóváhagyási felület, szerkesztés, átadás embernek.
- **Kiértékelés:** milyen példákon és milyen elfogadási feltételekkel mérik, és ki mondja ki, hogy kész.
- **Futó költség:** ki fizeti a modellhasználatot, és mi a becslés alapja.
- **Átadás:** kié a kód, a promptok és az értékelési példák, és van-e működtetési útmutató.
- **Megállási pont:** ki lehet-e szállni a felmérés vagy a prototípus után úgy, hogy az addigi eredmény használható.

Ha az egyik ajánlatból hiányzik a kiértékelés, az emberi ellenőrzés vagy a hibaágak kezelése, akkor nem olcsóbb, hanem kisebb munkát áraz.

### Milyen futó költségei vannak egy AI-megoldásnak indulás után?

Egy AI-megoldás futó költsége három tételből áll, és mindhárom a használattal együtt nő.

- **Modellhasználat.** A szolgáltató a feldolgozott szöveg mennyisége után számláz. A költség függ az esetek számától, a bemenetek hosszától, a választott modelltől, és attól, hány modellhívás kell egy feladathoz.
- **Monitorozás.** Valakinek rendszeresen mintát kell vennie a kimenetekből, figyelnie a hibákat és a visszajelzéseket, és modellcsere után újra le kell futtatnia az értékelési példákat.
- **A források karbantartása.** Ha változik egy ár, egy szabályzat vagy egy termékleírás, a tudásbázist frissíteni kell, különben a megoldás magabiztosan ad elavult választ. Ügyfélszolgálatnál ez különösen számít, erről az [AI ügyfélszolgálat emberi ellenőrzéssel](https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/irasok/ai-ugyfelszolgalat-emberi-ellenorzessel) cikk szól.

Számolj az ellenőrzésre fordított munkaidővel is: a jóváhagyó kolléga ideje költség, amelyet a megtérülésnél szembe kell állítani a megtakarított idővel.

### Összegzés

Az AI fejlesztés ára a feladat következménye. A folyamat terjedelme, az adatok állapota, az integrációk, az ellenőrzés és a kiértékelés szintje, a kockázat, a nyelvek és a karbantartás együtt határozza meg, és a legtöbbet az adatok rendbetételével és egy szűk első folyamattal tudsz spórolni. Ha leírod a folyamatot, az érintett rendszereket és azt, mi számítana sikernek, [küldd el](https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/kapcsolat), és megmondom, melyik szakasszal érdemes kezdeni.

### Források

- [Az Európai Parlament és a Tanács (EU) 2024/1689 rendelete (AI-rendelet), 50. cikk: átláthatósági kötelezettségek, ha az AI-rendszer természetes személyekkel lép kapcsolatba](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj), EUR-Lex, az Európai Unió Hivatalos Lapja, 2024. június 13., lekérve 2026. november 28-án

### Gyakori kérdések

#### Mennyibe kerül egy AI fejlesztés egy cégnek?

Az AI fejlesztés ára a folyamat terjedelmétől, az adatok állapotától, az integrációk számától, az emberi ellenőrzés és a kiértékelés szintjétől, a kockázattól, a nyelvektől és a karbantartástól függ. Fix árat nem mondok, mert minden megbízás egyedi munka. Pontos ajánlatot a felmérés után lehet adni.

#### Mi a különbség az AI integráció és az egyedi AI fejlesztés ára között?

Az AI integráció egy meglévő modellt köt be a folyamataidba és a rendszereidbe, az egyedi AI fejlesztés saját felületet, logikát vagy modellt is épít. Az integráció általában kisebb munka, de az adatok, az ellenőrzés és a kiértékelés költsége mindkettőnél megjelenik.

#### Hogyan lehet olcsóbban elkezdeni az AI bevezetést?

Egyetlen, szűk folyamattal, rendezett forrásokkal és olyan kapcsolattal, amely csak olvas. A felmérés és a prototípus kis kiadással megmutatja, megéri-e a pilot.

#### Miért tér el ennyire két AI fejlesztési ajánlat?

Mert ritkán árazzák ugyanazt a munkát. Az egyik egy modell bekötését tartalmazza, a másik az adat-előkészítést, az ellenőrző felületet, a kiértékelést és az átadást is. Kérd, hogy mindkettő tételesen írja le, mi van benne, és mi nincs.

#### Mennyi a havi költsége egy AI-megoldásnak?

A havi költség a modellhasználatból, a monitorozásból, a források karbantartásából és az ellenőrzésre fordított munkaidőből áll. A nagysága a használat mennyiségétől és a választott modelltől függ, ezért a pilot alatt érdemes megmérni.

---

## AI fejlesztő partner: 10 kérdés, mielőtt megbízod

- URL: https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/irasok/ai-fejleszto-partner-valasztasa
- Language: Hungarian
- Published: 2026-11-27; updated: 2026-11-28
- Author: Norbert Barna (https://www.linkedin.com/in/barna-norbert/)
- Also available in English: https://www.barnanorbert.com/writing/before-hiring-an-ai-integration-partner; German: https://www.barnanorbert.com/de/wissen/ki-dienstleister-auswaehlen
- Summary: Mit kérdezz egy AI fejlesztő partnertől a megbízás előtt: öt dolog, amit előre készíts elő, és tíz kérdés a jó válasz ismérveivel.

Egy AI fejlesztő partnertől a megbízás előtt azt kérdezd meg, mit tesztelne, mielőtt bármit építene, hogyan méri a kimenet minőségét a te valódi eseteiden, mi történik a felületen, ha az AI téved, kik dolgoznak a projekten, és kié lesz a rendszer az átadás után. Előtte készíts elő öt dolgot: egy folyamatot, annak mai kiinduló értékét, az érintett adatokat és rendszereket, azt, hogy mi marad emberi döntés, és a mérőszámot, amely eldönti, folytatódik-e a pilot. Ezekkel az első beszélgetésből körülhatárolt ajánlat lesz, nélkülük egy demó.

Ez a cikk két listát ad: mit vigyél magaddal az első egyeztetésre, és mit kérdezz ott, a jó válasz ismérveivel együtt. Tizenhét éve dolgozom szabályozott termékeken (banki, vállalati biztonsági és vállalati EdTech rendszereken), és a listák a saját projektjeimből állnak össze, nem piaci felmérésből.

### Röviden: hogyan válassz AI fejlesztő partnert

- **Öt dolgot vigyél az első egyeztetésre:** egy folyamat leírását, a mai kiinduló értékét, az érintett adatok és rendszerek listáját, azt, hogy mi marad emberi döntés, és a mérőszámot, amely a pilot folytatásáról dönt.
- **A legfontosabb kérdés:** „Mit tesztelnél, mielőtt bármit építesz?” A jó válasz megnevez egy feltevést, egy próbát a te anonimizált eseteiden, és azt az eredményt, amelynél a partner azt javasolná, hogy ne építsetek semmit.
- **Döntési szabály:** azt a partnert válaszd, aki írásban, a te folyamatodra vonatkoztatva válaszol a tíz kérdésre. Ha a demó előbb jön, mint a kérdések a folyamatodról, keress tovább.
- **Tulajdon:** az átadás után a kód, a promptok, a tesztkészlet és a dokumentáció a tiéd, a szolgáltatói fiókok a te nevedben futnak. Ezt a szerződés előtt rögzítsd írásban.
- **Adat:** az első beszélgetéshez elég a folyamat egyoldalas, anonimizált leírása. Jelszót és ügyféladatot ne küldj, amíg a megosztás módja nincs írásban rögzítve.

### Miért az előkészítésen múlik, milyen ajánlatot kapsz?

Előkészítés nélkül egy AI fejlesztő csak azt tudja megmutatni, mire képes egy modell, és nagyjából minden partner modellje ugyanarra képes. Ha viszont viszel egy folyamatot és egy kiinduló értéket, a partnernek arról kell beszélnie, mi változik a te munkádban, hogyan, és miből fogod ezt látni. Ez a beszélgetés választja szét azokat, akik valódi működésbe építenek AI-t, azoktól, akik demót adnak el. A megnevezés mellékes: az AI tanácsadás, az AI fejlesztés és az AI integráció mögött ugyanazt a próbát érdemes elvégezni.

### Mit készíts elő, mielőtt AI fejlesztő partnert keresel?

1. **Egy folyamat, azoknak a szavaival, akik végzik.** Válassz egy ismétlődő feladatot, és írasd le a munkatársakkal a bemeneteket, az átadási pontokat, a visszatérő döntéseket és azt, mibe kerül egy hiba. A kiválasztáshoz öt szempontot ad a [melyik folyamattal kezdj](https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/irasok/ai-automatizalas-melyik-folyamattal-kezdj) cikk.
2. **Kiinduló érték.** Mennyi ideig tart ma egy eset, milyen gyakori a hiba, mennyi a várakozás, a saját nyilvántartásodból. Ha nincs ilyen adatod, ez az első feladat, még a partner megbízása előtt. Kiinduló érték nélkül később senki sem tudja megmondani, segített-e a pilot.
3. **Adatok és hozzáférés.** Melyik rendszerben van az adat, melyik adat használható, hova kerülhet információ, és ki hagyja jóvá a hozzáférést. Jelszót, ügyféladatot vagy bizalmas anyagot ne küldj senkinek, amíg nincs megegyezés a megosztás módjáról. Az első beszélgetéshez elég a folyamat egyoldalas, anonimizált leírása.
4. **Ami emberi döntés marad.** Mit javasolhat az AI, mit kell embernek ellenőriznie, és mi történik, ha a válasz hiányzik vagy hibás. A felületi mintákat a [Human in the loop: hét minta](https://www.barnanorbert.com/hu/irasok/human-in-the-loop-emberi-felugyelet) cikkben írom le.
5. **Sikermérőszám és felelős.** Melyik mérőszám dönt a pilot folytatásáról (elvégzett feladatok, ellenőrzésre fordított idő, kimeneti minőség, válaszidő vagy futási költség), a kiinduló értékhez mérve. Mellé egy megnevezett ember a te oldaladon, aki a pilotot szüneteltetheti vagy visszavonhatja.

Írd össze a korlátaidat is: nyelvek, szabályozott adatok, akadálymentességi követelmények, beszerzési szabályok.
